World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: As Ebola Spreads to 8th DR Congo Province, Families Battle to Feed Themselves
World.content:
A health worker carries a stretcher into an Ebola treatment centre in the DR Congo.

Geneva — Hunger in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) is undermining efforts to combat Ebola as the deadly disease has expanded across borders and also to an eighth province of the huge central African country, the UN said on Friday.

Families facing Ebola in the DR Congo, which has a population of more than 105 million, can find that protecting themselves from the virus can also mean losing the means to feed their children, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).

“Today, the outbreak has spread to an eighth province, reaching communities already under immense pressure,” David Stevenson, the WFP's DRC country director, said during a UN press conference.

“As it spreads, hunger continues to undermine the measures needed to contain it.”

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

And earlier in the week, the World Health Organisation (WHO), on Oct. 20, said that Nigeria has confirmed one imported case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

It became the fifth country to detect the virus since the DRC declared an outbreak on May 15.

The spread of the disease comes as agencies fighting the escalating Ebola virus in the DRC constantly battle to win the trust of local communities, according to international groups in the field calling for the protection of health workers.

Stevenson said that the WFP has two critical roles: helping families seek care without sacrificing food and providing the logistics backbone that keeps the wider response moving.

“Without sustained support, we risk leaving families unable to follow health guidance when it matters most.”

The WFP official explained that in Ituri’s Mungbwalu, the epicentre of the outbreak, Francine Birungi Amoti has lost a child to Ebola.

“She is raising her six surviving children and another baby entrusted to her care. Violence has cut her off from her fields.

“She told me, ‘If you go, you may not even return alive, and I do not have money to buy food at the local market. So we stay at home, and WFP helps us enormously.’”

For Francine, food assistance means feeding the children in her care when reaching her fields could cost her life.

'INSECURITY AND HUNGER'

“This is what a crisis on top of a crisis looks like: disease and bereavement, compounded by insecurity and hunger,” said Stevenson.

He also cited the case in North-Kivu’s Butembo, where Isabelle Kyakimwa arrived at an Ebola treatment centre without strength.

“As she recovered, she told us: ‘Food is important for us as patients because it helps us regain the strength to keep going.’

Close 

Her words show what food assistance brings to a treatment centre: regular, safe, nutritious meals that support recovery, dignity, and continuity of care.

“Food does not treat Ebola. Medical teams do,” said Stevenson.

“But their work takes place amid severe food insecurity and continued violence that repeatedly displaces families, destroys livelihoods and complicates access to care.”

He said food assistance is vital to supporting patients through that care and that WFP needs $115 million over the next six months, including $79 million for hot meals and dry rations.

World.title: Kenya: Calls for Penalties Follow 12-Story Building Collapse
World.content:
A building under construction collapsed in the Eastleigh neighborhood of Nairobi.

Nairobi — Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has called for tougher penalties against rogue developers and the restoration of prosecutorial powers to county governments following the collapse of an incomplete 12-storey building in Eastleigh.

Sakaja said weak penalties for violating construction regulations undermine enforcement efforts and allow developers to compromise building safety, putting lives at risk.

Speaking as he led multi-agency rescue operations at the site along 1st Avenue, 9th Street, the Governor urged professional bodies representing architects, engineers and quantity surveyors to take action against developers who dismiss qualified experts after obtaining construction approvals.



He said some developers engage licensed professionals to secure approvals but subsequently remove them from projects and proceed with construction using unqualified personnel, undermining safeguards intended to ensure buildings meet approved designs and safety standards.

"We have formally written to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, and we hope our request will be considered. Counties must be empowered to take firm action against rogue developers who disregard building regulations and put lives at risk," Sakaja said.

The Governor questioned the deterrent effect of existing penalties, noting that some developers found guilty of violating construction regulations could face fines as low as Sh5,000.

"Even when such offenders are arrested and taken to court, the penalties can be as low as Sh5,000, which is not a sufficient deterrent," he said.

Sakaja argued that restoring prosecutorial powers to county governments would strengthen enforcement and enable authorities to take firmer action against developers who disregard approved construction plans and safety requirements.

He called on professional associations representing architects, engineers, quantity surveyors and builders to collaborate with county governments in identifying and investigating cases where qualified professionals are withdrawn from construction sites under questionable circumstances.

The Governor said the bodies should take appropriate disciplinary action against professionals found culpable, adding that experts responsible for building design, supervision and safety must be allowed to discharge their duties without interference.

Sakaja also reiterated the need for developers to obtain occupation certificates before putting buildings into use. He said structures must undergo the necessary inspections to establish that they are safe and fit for occupation.

According to the Governor, developers are required to secure county approvals, engage qualified professionals and sign indemnity forms committing them to comply with approved plans and construction standards.

However, he said some developers disregard these commitments after obtaining approvals, compromising the integrity of construction projects.

The calls for stronger enforcement came after an incomplete 12-storey building collapsed in Eastleigh, triggering a multi-agency search and rescue operation amid fears that people were trapped beneath the rubble.

The building was still under construction, with the ground floor occupied at the time of the collapse.

Nairobi City County emergency response teams were coordinating operations alongside the National Disaster Operations Centre, the Kenya Red Cross, the Kenya Defence Forces and other agencies.

Heavy machinery had been deployed to clear debris and create access to sections where victims could be trapped, as additional resources were mobilised to support the rescue effort.

Sakaja urged families and members of the public with information about missing persons to report to designated centres established by rescue teams at the scene.

Close 

Residents were also advised to share information through the county's emergency hotlines, 1508 and 1199.

"Our health teams are on standby to provide immediate medical attention and support rescue efforts as soon as victims are reached. We are doing everything possible to ensure the operation proceeds as quickly and safely as possible," he said.

The collapse has renewed scrutiny of building safety enforcement in Nairobi, particularly compliance with approved construction plans, the engagement of qualified professionals and inspections at different stages of development.

Sakaja said stronger legal powers, tougher penalties and closer collaboration between county governments and professional bodies were necessary to hold developers accountable and prevent similar incidents.

He maintained that restoring county prosecutorial powers would complement existing inspection and enforcement mechanisms by strengthening the ability of local authorities to pursue violations of construction regulations.

World.title: Rwanda: Kagame Defends Strict Dress Codes Amid Rwanda's Dressing Controversy
World.content:
Rwandan President Paul Kagame has defended cultural expectations on dressing, arguing that societies have their own standards of acceptable behaviour which should not be abandoned simply because other countries embrace different ways of life.

Speaking on Thursday while addressing more than 10,000 young Rwandans at BK Arena in Kigali during the "Meet The President" session, Kagame said dress codes should be understood within the context of the places people visit and the values of the society in which they live.

"If you are going to the beach, by the water, where people go to relax, there is a certain way you can dress and behave that may be different from other places. That is perfectly acceptable. But imagine someone coming here dressed as though they were at the beach. Would that work? Wouldn't you all turn around and wonder, what happened to this person?" Kagame asked.



His remarks come amid a growing debate in Rwanda over restrictions on women's dressing, following incidents in which women have faced scrutiny over their clothing in public spaces.

The debate intensified after a video circulated showing police officers forcefully handcuffing a young woman wearing a miniskirt at a bus park in Rubavu.

The Rwanda National Police subsequently cleared the woman of wrongdoing and detained the officers involved pending disciplinary review.

The incident also drew criticism from human rights advocates and public commentators, who argued that cultural values should not be used to justify police intimidation, harassment or arbitrary enforcement of dress standards against women.

Addressing the wider debate, Kagame said the expectations should apply to men as well, arguing that discussions about dressing are often unfairly directed at women.

"By the way, this is not just about women. Most of the time, these things are made to be about women, but the same applies to men. Even now, imagine we are sitting here, and a man suddenly walks in, as though he has just come from the gym, wearing shorts, with nothing on his upper body, and comes to sit among us. People would ask, what happened to this person? Did he forget where he was going?" he said.

Kagame argued that societies should be allowed to maintain their own social standards rather than adopt practices from other countries without considering whether they fit local values.

He said people's willingness to participate in a particular social setting could also depend on the expectations established by those organising it.

"Now, if we had all agreed to come dressed that way, then perhaps that is how it would be. But some people would not come. Isn't that so? Some would simply decide not to attend, saying, we are not going to be part of that," he said.

The Rwandan leader said communities have ways of regulating behaviour through shared expectations and self-regulation, adding that practices accepted elsewhere should not automatically be embraced by Rwandans.

"There is a way society regulates itself, including through self-regulation. But when you simply say, we have seen this elsewhere, so let us do the same here, and you bring it into our society, society may tell you, we have not reached that point yet. Perhaps we were moving in that direction, but we are not there yet," Kagame said.

He called for disagreements over cultural values to be handled through dialogue rather than hostility, saying people should be able to reach an understanding when differences emerge.

"That should not create any hostility. There should be a way of regulating these things so that people can come to an understanding," he said.

Kagame compared society's response to unfamiliar practices to the body's reaction to a foreign object, which it gradually attempts to remove.

"It is like a foreign body. I think those of you in the medical profession know this. When a foreign object, a fragment of something, enters the body, the body tends to reject it. It keeps pushing it out. Even when a thorn gets stuck in your skin, if you leave it there for some time, it begins to work its way out. Eventually, you find it near the surface and remove it. Society works in much the same way," he said.

He added that tensions can arise when individuals seek to introduce practices that conflict with the established values of a community, while other members of that society resist the changes.

"A healthy society, with its own way of functioning, when something unfamiliar is introduced into it, gradually, little by little, that society begins to push it away. There is then a struggle between someone trying to change society to fit something they have brought from elsewhere, and society itself saying, do not bring these things here, and pushing that person away. But there should be no conflict. That is how these things should work," Kagame said.

Close 

He urged young people to reflect on the values they want for themselves and the direction in which they want their society to develop.

"Young people like you should keep these things in mind. Think about them. Understand what it is that you want for yourselves," he said.

Kagame also called for open discussions about changing social norms, urging young Rwandans to question practices that are becoming more common but which they consider inconsistent with their culture or harmful to society.

"Even here, in our discussions, people should be able to raise these questions and say, there are things we have seen becoming increasingly accepted in our society, yet they are not part of our culture. They do not even bring us any benefit. Why should we accept them, especially when they are things that harm people? Why?" he asked.

World.title: Nigeria: Health Is Economic Infrastructure - Why Nigeria Must Invest in Health
World.content:
blog

Listen to this article 8 min The recently concluded World Health Summit in Berlin, themed "From Crisis to Resilience: Innovating for Health", reinforced a key message: health spending is an investment, not just an expense. Yet Nigeria's 2026 Appropriation Bill proposed ₦2.48 trillion for health out of ₦58.47 trillion, about 4.2% of the budget. That is less than a third of the 15% target African governments agreed to in the 2001 Abuja Declaration.

Closing this gap requires recognising health as an investment in economic growth, much like roads and power. Nigeria's growth ambitions depend on people being healthy enough to participate in the economy. Health should therefore be treated as economic infrastructure in the country's development priorities and budget decisions.

What the evidence actually supports



Egypt's experience illustrates the potential economic returns of health investment. At the summit session Funding the Future: Unlocking the Economic and Fiscal Returns of Health Innovation, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Egypt's Minister of Health and Population, described a $240 million early-detection programme reaching 60 million people, followed by affordable generic treatment. It was projected to save $7 billion by 2030, a 688% return.

However, these are projections, not a confirmed result. For Nigeria, achieving comparable gains would require screening capacity and reliable medicine supplies that are not yet available at the same scale. Martin Seychell, Deputy Director-General at DG INTPA at the European Commission, cautioned that better outcomes depend on how the money is spent.

"We should not make the mistake of simply gauging and assessing efforts simply on the basis of how much money we are investing in health budgets. Because we know, of course, if you underinvest, you will not get good outcomes. But it doesn't follow that if you just increase the health budgets without a clear strategy, you will get better outcomes."

Nigeria's clearest return is household income

One of the clearest benefits for Nigeria is the funds families could keep if healthcare were more affordable. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO, Amref Health Africa singled out Nigeria when discussing the high out-of-pocket health expenditure, noting that what people pay out of pocket is "ridiculously higher than the government spends."

People pay about 71.9% of current health expenditure out of pocket. An analysis of the 2023/24 General Household Survey found that 45.5% of households faced catastrophic health spending, meaning health costs accounted for at least 10% of their household budget. These bills can force families to borrow, sell belongings or cut spending on food and education.

During the Strategic Health Economy session, Dr Ezekwesili recalled that evidence showing that malaria cost Africa about 2% of its GDP "changed the conversation" with ministers and described the disease as a "productivity tax on the economies." The Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare estimates that malaria reduces Nigeria's GDP by more than $1.1 billion each year, while Nigeria accounts for 27% of global cases.

At the same session, Dr Satoshi Ezoe, Japan's Assistant Minister for Global Health, explained that Japan reached universal health coverage in 1961 while still recovering from the Second World War, and argued that "we laid the foundation by making UHC, which led to socioeconomic development."

Nigeria is one of the first eight countries in the UHC Knowledge Hub, a Japanese initiative with the World Health Organization and the World Bank that brings health and finance ministries together to plan for universal coverage. Successful coverage should mean fewer families are pushed into hardship by medical bills and fewer workdays lost, not enrolment figures alone.

Who captures the value?

The economic case for health investment extends to building local industries and creating employment opportunities. Yet Africa captures little of the value from the health products it uses, as Dr Obiageli Ezekwesili, founder and chief executive officer of Human Capital Africa, told the summit during the session The Strategic Health Economy:

"[Africa's] capacity in terms of... global manufacturing... it's less than 5%. Then you look at... competitiveness... how much value does Africa gain from the health value chain -- also insignificant...

Nigeria aims to increase local production of essential health products to 70% by 2030. The Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain is supported by tax and duty waivers on pharmaceutical inputs and about $2 billion in financing commitments.

However, packaging imported products locally is not the same as making them locally. Manufacturers still rely on imported active pharmaceutical ingredients to produce medicines, leaving them exposed to foreign-exchange fluctuations and price volatility.

Local production also needs skilled workers, as does the wider health system. Nigeria has 95,456 registered doctors but only 60,551 with active practising licenses, while its 2024 National Policy on Health Workforce Migration requires wider implementation.

The role of policy in enabling health workers to deliver care also features in the summit session Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century, where Dr Githinji Gitahi, Group CEO of Amref Health Africa, stressed its importance for community health workers.

Making investment accountable

Funding also must reach the services it is meant for. At the Health as an Investment: Preparing Systems & Societies for the 21st Century session, Dr Gitahi warned that prevention and vaccination budgets "are the first to be cut" when fiscal space tightens, because their results are less visible.

Nigeria shows the risk: in 2025, only ₦36 million of the ₦218 billion appropriated for federal health capital projects was released. For Nigeria, the value of health investment lies in the industries it builds and the workers it equips. Realising that value requires funding, procurement and regulation to support these goals.

Close 

The following steps could help put this into practice;

The Office of the Accountant-General and Budget Office should include health infrastructure in quarterly cash plans and publish how much funding is released.

The National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) and state schemes should automatically enrol eligible conditional cash transfer beneficiaries and publish whether enrolment reduces their out-of-pocket spending. In addition, the NHIA, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), and state governments could consider offering qualified Nigerian manufacturers multi-year purchasing agreements with clear standards for price, quality, and delivery. Reliable demand would make it easier for manufacturers to invest.

Incentives under the Presidential Initiative for Unlocking the Healthcare Value Chain (PVAC) and NAFDAC approval pathways should reward verified local production, including making ingredients and meeting quality standards. Annual reporting should show which products are replacing imports.

Health belongs in Nigeria's growth strategy for the same reason ports and power do: the economy depends on it. That case must be reflected in funding released on time, stronger local production and affordable, quality care. Nigeria needs to spend more on health, use the funds strategically and measure whether people and the economy are better off.

World.title: South Africa: How Nurses Are Learning to Administer the New HIV Prevention Injection
World.content:
South Africa's rollout of lenacapavir, a six-monthly HIV prevention injection, requires nurses to learn, adapt and find ways to make it work for patients.

After 26 years in nursing, Sister Keitumetse "Tumi" Senokwane still had something new to learn about giving injections.

The six-monthly HIV-prevention jab, lenacapavir, often referred to as just LEN, presented a unique challenge.

"You know, lenacapavir is different. As much as I've got experience with injections, the needle size is different from the subcutaneous (beneath the skin) injections we are used to, and the solution is quite thick," says Senokwane. "Because we were not used to it, the practical training helped us to get used to it." She practised withdrawing the yellow liquid, using cooking oil as a stand-in.



That kind of preparation matters because lenacapavir for HIV prevention is being introduced at a time when South Africa still has a substantial need for effective HIV prevention options. The country had an estimated 140 000 new HIV infections in 2025. Modelling suggests that scaling up lenacapavir to 1.4 million to 2.1 million initiations a year by 2030 could avert an average of 32 200 to 51 700 infections annually.

But realising lenacapavir's potential will depend on more than getting the injection into clinics. It also requires nurses to administer it correctly, answer patients' questions, and adapt services to their needs.

Getting to grips with lenacapavir

Senokwane is a professional nurse and site manager at Maria Rantho Community Health Centre and Phedisong 1 Clinic in Tshwane, which are participating in the Wits RHI Len4PrEP study.

"LEN4PrEP is an implementation research study, so looking at how we can deliver the product in a real-world setting," says study investigator Dr Catherine Martin.

The researchers recruited 1 544 participants between November 2025 and June 2026, with follow-up continuing until June 2027. The study began several months before South Africa's national rollout of lenacapavir on 5 June 2026, when the injection was launched at 360 public health facilities across six provinces.

By 8 October, 76 922 people had initiated LEN nationally, including 36 733 in 133 facilities in Gauteng, according to health department spokesperson Foster Mohale.

For Senokwane and her colleagues, administering lenacapavir meant learning a new HIV prevention method.

Nurses first had to complete a compulsory Nurse-Initiated Management of Antiretroviral Therapy (NIMART) course, which provides a theoretical foundation for managing HIV and antiretroviral treatment. This was followed by practical training in preparing and administering LEN.

Training also covered eligibility, side effects, HIV testing and counselling, with videos and clinical mentorship providing additional support.

Mohale says feedback from early-rollout clinics, nurses and patients would help the department refine its training and guidelines.

At the study clinics, nurses also had to adapt the service to patients' needs and fit the new injection method into existing care.

The one-stop shop

The Department of Health's lenacapavir implementation guidelines emphasise counselling clients on their HIV prevention options and helping them choose a method that suits their needs.

At the study clinics, nurses incorporated LEN into existing sexual and reproductive health services, allowing clients to access HIV prevention alongside services such as family planning and STI screening and treatment during a single visit.

"You will get all services in one room like a one-stop shop," says Senokwane.

"Maybe you are here for lenacapavir, but we also check whether you are on a family planning method. If not, we will give you information and provide a family planning method for you, where we screen you for STIs, and then if you've got some infections, we also treat you," she says.

The LEN4PrEP study also used a mobile clinic to bring HIV prevention and sexual and reproductive health services to young people in their communities.

"So many of our clients already know us. They know how we treat them and the quality of service we provide," she says.

Initial LEN consultations took longer as nurses explained the available prevention methods and how soon each would offer protection against HIV.

"We give you the information and explain how each method works, how long until it is effective. Participants would like to know when they are going to be protected from HIV if they take this specific method," says Senokwane.

At the Southern African HIV Clinicians Society's Long-Acting Antiretroviral Treatment Conference in Johannesburg in September, Wits RHI's Professor Saiqa Mullick, Director of Implementation Science, shared early findings from the LEN4PrEP study.

She reported that convenience was a major reason participants opted for the lenacapavir jab. They valued not having to take a daily pill or make frequent clinic visits, while the injection offered greater privacy for some. It also attracted people new to PrEP, alongside existing users seeking a method that better suited their lives.

Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, refers to antiretroviral medicines taken to prevent HIV infection. When used as prescribed, oral PrEP has been shown to reduce the risk of HIV infection from sex. For several years now, HIV prevention tablets have been widely available in South Africa's public healthcare system, although uptake has been somewhat muted with only around 350 000 people taking the tablets in mid-2025, according to estimates from Thembisa, the leading mathematical model of HIV in South Africa.

Of the 1 538 participants whose method choices were reported, 85.8% selected the lenacapavir shot, compared with 13.7% who selected the prevention pills and 0.5% who chose not to use PrEP.

"People want options that fit into their lives," Mullick told delegates.

Sticking the landing

Patients could also choose where in the body to receive the injections: the upper arm, buttocks, abdomen or thigh.

Among the 1 319 participants who started LEN, Mullick says approximately 50% of women preferred the buttocks, while about 51% of men preferred the upper arm. The ongoing study will explore both men and women's reasons for injection-site preferences.

For nurses, the challenge was to administer the injections correctly while making the process as efficient as possible.

Lenacapavir requires getting two injections during the same visit. Patients also need to take two lenacapavir tablets on the day of their first injections, followed by another two tablets 24 hours later. These tablets form part of the initiation dose before they continue with injections every six months.

Senokwane says a Wits RHI pharmacist taught her a way to withdraw the solution while keeping the vial upright, rather than turning it upside down.

"That was the best method for me because it worked faster," says Senokwane.

"So with that method, you pull up 1.5 ml of air into the syringe and inject the needle into the vial. [The syringe] draws at least one ml by itself, without assistance, which allows the nurse to multitask. And then you also save time because you are able to prepare two injections at the same time," she says.

But efficiency was only part of the learning curve. Because lenacapavir is a thick solution, it needs to be injected slowly.

"I wish I knew that you can't inject it fast," Senokwane said. The thick solution required a slower injection technique to reduce leakage.

Slow administration was included in nurses' initial training, but its importance in minimising leakage was reinforced as they gained practical experience and shared lessons with colleagues.

Dr Martin says that in the early stages of implementation, nurses consulted experts, including those involved in clinical trials, on how to manage leakage at the injection site.

"As local experience grew, they learnt to reassure participants that minor leakage could occur and to assess more substantial leakage to determine whether further follow-up was needed."

Answering patient concerns

Patients were also concerned about the side effects of lenacapavir.

Lumps or small nodules at the injection site are a common side effect of lenacapavir. In one clinical trial, which included 2 140 participants who received lenacapavir, roughly 64% developed subcutaneous nodules at the injection site.

"Most of the clients were curious about the nodules. They were worried about whether they would be able to continue with their normal activities, especially those who wanted to exercise," says Senokwane.

"They wanted to know how long the nodule would last and whether they would get another one when they came back for their second injection. Usually, by the time they came for their next injection, the nodule would have disappeared."

Others were worried about the pain.

"We advise them that if the nodule comes with pain, just use a warm or cold compress, or you can even use a painkiller," explains Senokwane.

Mullick says addressing these concerns and discussing them with clients in advance is part of making the injection work for patients in practice.

"This might seem something relatively small, but from an implementation perspective, it contributes considerably to the person receiving the product."

Close 

Making it work in real time

As nurses became more familiar with administering lenacapavir, the clinics also refined how they moved patients through the service, from the initial consultation to receiving the injection.

Patients first met a navigator who explained the available services. After registration, an HIV test and a check of their vital signs, they saw the research nurse.

The clinics later began using the waiting time more effectively, with navigators introducing patients to PrEP and other services before their consultations.

Initially, appointments could take about an hour and a half. As the clinics refined their workflow and nurses became more familiar with the process, Senokwane says visits took about an hour or less.

"Training manuals and guidelines provide all the theoretical knowledge and framework for delivering lenacapavir," Martin explains.

"But, that real-world experience gives you a little bit more insight into things that you can only learn by working with clients."

Each one teach one

Senokwane's experience eventually helped her become a mentor to other nurses.

"The mentorship was really very important. We've got support from our pharmacist, and then we've got support from our sub-investigator at site. So everyone needs to be mentored until you are really 100% sure that you can do it on your own," she says.

When non-research nurses started providing lenacapavir in June at the study sites, she went there to demonstrate the technique. Some nurses she had trained also helped their colleagues.

"They were always grateful that we really helped them. So they really appreciated it. The more you practice, the better you become," says Senokwane.

Lessons from the clinics also informed training. Videos demonstrating how to prepare and administer lenacapavir were produced by Wits RHI, alongside webinars. Martin says the videos would be incorporated into future training.

"It's always helpful to see something in practice. With a new product, although it can be explained theoretically, it is helpful to actually see a provider and a client interaction," she says.

World.title: Malawi: Schools Urged to Adapt As Heatwave Warning Issued Across Malawi
World.content:
Schools and other learning institutions have been urged to implement immediate measures to protect learners and staff following a heatwave alert issued by the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS).

The Department has forecast temperatures of up to 42C in parts of the Southern Region, with unusually high temperatures also expected across the Central, Northern and lakeshore areas.

In a statement, Secretary for Education Dr Ken Ndala said institutions should strictly adhere to precautionary measures aimed at safeguarding learners, teachers and support staff while maintaining continuity in education.

Schools have been advised to adjust timetables, relax uniform requirements and adopt flexible learning arrangements where necessary to reduce exposure to extreme heat.



The ministry has also directed institutions to suspend or reschedule outdoor activities, including sports, assemblies, parades and manual work, during the hottest part of the day, between 10am and 3pm.

Additional guidance includes ensuring continuous access to safe drinking water, encouraging regular hydration, keeping classrooms cool and well-ventilated, making use of shaded areas and avoiding overcrowding.

Schools have also been asked to pay particular attention to vulnerable groups, including young children, people with albinism, pregnant members of staff and those living with chronic health conditions.

"The ministry also reminds institutions to make use of the El Niño Practical Guidance for the Education Sector 2026-2027 booklets that have been distributed to strengthen preparedness and response to climate-related hazards," the statement said.

The advisory forms part of wider efforts to minimise the impact of extreme weather conditions on learning and to reduce health risks associated with prolonged exposure to high temperatures.

World.title: After yet another inexcusable loss to Wisconsin, the Lincoln Riley era at USC looks to be nearing an end
World.content:
How quickly things can change in the world of modern college football.

Just a few weeks ago, the USC Trojans were seemingly riding a wave of positive momentum. In the Lincoln Riley era, SC has struggled to win on the road, particularly against traditionally big programs. In 2025, for example, the Trojans went 9-3 in the regular season, with all three losses coming at Illinois, at Oregon and at Notre Dame.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But things were supposed to be different in 2026. SC brought in the number one recruiting class in the country. They brought back starting quarterback Jayden Maiava, entering his third year in the program and second full season as the starter. New defensive coordinator Gary Patterson brought a wealth of experience and a history of getting elite performance out of TCU level talent.

LINCOLN RILEY HOT SEAT RUMORS GET LOUDER AFTER 'FIRE LINCOLN' CHANTS DURING USC-WASHINGTON

While the schedule looked daunting, thanks to games against Oregon, Penn State, Ohio State and Indiana, 2026 was widely viewed as a turning point for the program. Win 10 games and make the College Football Playoff, or bust. Through early October, despite some underwhelming performances, the Trojans were squarely in position.

Chaos throughout the SEC opened the door for more available at-large spots. Despite an ugly home loss to a diminished Oregon team, SC was 5-1 heading into a big road game against Penn State. And finally, a Riley-coached SC team looked prepared. Even with the "White Out" home crowd, a motivated PSU team, the lengthy road trip to the Eastern Time Zone, and a long litany of injuries, SC won 31-23 ahead of their bye week.

In the interim, Ohio State lost their starting quarterback Julian Sayin, likely for the remainder of the regular season, making their matchup on Halloween look a lot more winnable. SC just had to get through another road game at Wisconsin to set up the biggest home game in years. And boy oh boy did they not get through it.

Almost immediately, the Trojans looked the way they so frequently have under Riley: poorly coached, undisciplined, and unable to overcome when things start going against them. Their offensive line, which was supposed to be a strength, was confused and overwhelmed by a Wisconsin defense that allowed 41 points to Notre Dame. Maiava played one of his worst games as a Trojan, throwing two interceptions, though one was on a deflected pass, and taking multiple awful intentional grounding penalties. One of which set up a much longer field goal attempt, which was promptly blocked.

USC's running game was nonexistent, with minus-17 total yards thanks to Maiava's minus-57 — minus-57!!! — rushing yards. There were multiple drops by the receiving corps. Perhaps most emblematic was the sequence that played out late in the second quarter.

Wisconsin had a nearly eight-minute touchdown drive, kicking the ball back to SC with the Badgers up 10-7, 1:51 remaining and the Trojans still with all three timeouts. Boobie Feaster muffed the kickoff at the goal line, however, and SC started their drive at their own 7-yard-line. After five plays and a first down, they ended the half at the ... 8-yard line.

Then in the second half, Riley made a series of indefensible mistakes.

The Badgers started the third quarter by driving down to the USC 16-yard line, but the Trojans' defense held, setting up a fourth-and-2. Wisconsin came out in an unusual formation, with four wide receivers bunched toward the sideline. Riley decided against calling a timeout, even though his defense wasn't aligned properly, with just two defensive backs on four receivers, and multiple players covering no one in the middle of the field. Predictably, the play resulted in a Wisconsin touchdown, extending their lead to 17-7.

SC's drive to start the fourth quarter was equally bad. The Trojans moved the ball down to the Wisconsin 33-yard line, before Maiava took a sack on second down to make it third-and-20. SC picked up eight to set up a lengthy, 53-yard field goal attempt. A substitution-based delay of game penalty made it fourth-and-17 from the 41-yard-line, and instead of punting, or even just throwing a screen pass to pick up yardage with a slight chance of a first down, Riley chose to attempt a 59-yard field goal. Predictably, it came up about 10 yards short.

The Badgers drove down the field immediately afterward for the back-breaking, game-ending touchdown that not only gave SC their second loss, but seemingly put a bow on Riley's time in Los Angeles.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Not all the blame for the loss goes on Riley; Maiava was awful, looking hurried, flustered and frequently making poor decisions. The offensive line was atrocious, giving up pressure after pressure and flailing helplessly in the run game too. Once again, the SC defense just wasn't good enough, despite the Badgers' one-dimensional offensive "attack."

Wisconsin averaged just 3.5 yards per play, with only 200 total yards. They had 58 — 58! — total passing yards. Wisconsin barely even attempted plays other than inside or outside zone handoffs or designed quarterback runs. And SC still allowed three touchdown drives.

Explanations for this individual game aside, it's the result that's once again indefensible. Wisconsin is nowhere close to the level of Ohio State, Indiana, Georgia, Notre Dame or other top teams, and SC's offense was completely overmatched anyway. Seven points was the fewest scored by any Riley-coached team. Ever. In year five, it's the same mistakes, over and over again and a defense that can't win games when the offense struggles. Indiana escaped over Michigan 13-6, because their defense can get stops when they need them. That's never been the case for a Riley-coached SC team.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

SC still has an opportunity to reach the playoffs if they beat Ohio State, Indiana, Maryland and UCLA. But it's impossible to believe they'll win those four games. It's hard to believe they'll win more than two. Which sets up yet another disappointing 8-4 or, at best, 9-3 season. For all the money that's been dumped into the program, that's not good enough.

John Harbaugh was passing out credit for Sunday's overtime win against the Houston Texans immediately after the game. And the New York Giants coach said the credit goes to the players, including quarterback J.J. McCarthy and running back Cam Skattebo, and God.

"First of all, I just want to humbly say, just personally, very grateful to my Lord, High Rock, Protector and Stronghold, the Lord God in heaven," Harbaugh said in opening his news conference. "And our guys, man, that was a player's win."

The Giants are supposed to win this season with their young quarterback and young running back doing incredible things, but who could've predicted McCarthy would be the young quarterback instead of Jaxson Dart, and the young running back would have to get out of the coaching staff's doghouse first.

JAXSON DART TORE HIS MCL AND MENISCUS WHICH REQUIRE SURGERY AND ENDS HIS 2026 SEASON WITH THE NEW YORK GIANTS

McCarthy and Skattebo were outstanding in helping the Giants beat the Texans.

Skattebo rushed for a career-high 124 yards, delivered perhaps the game's defining run in overtime to set up the winning points, and ran so hard throughout the game – get this – on one play he was flagged for unnecessary roughness.

Because he buried an potential tackler.

NFL REFS HAVE SET ALL-TIME RECORD FOR FLAGS THIS SEASON, AND IT'S CHANGING THE OUTCOME OF GAMES

On New York's second possession, Skattebo took a handoff from McCarthy and drove through a hole, lowered his head, and ran through Texans safety M.J. Stewart.

Skattebo steamrolled Stewart but the NFL is all about player safety these days so he was flagged because he lowered his head before making contact.

Larry Csonka, Jim Brown and Earl Campbell would have been proud. And the 15 yard penalty that followed would have been foreign and appalling to the all time greats.

Skattebo wasn't done. He scored on a 16-yard run and in overtime got off a 42-yard run that gave the Giants the football at the Houston 28 yard line. A field goal would have won it from there, but Devin Singletary ran in for a TD on the next play and a Giants win.

Harbaugh, who benched Skattebo last week, said his running back played with a "fierce joy" on Sunday.

The coach also noted how McCarthy responded in his start to deliver his first win as the Giants starting quarterback. McCarthy was officially named the starter on Wednesday, succeeding Jameis Winston who had succeeded the injured Dart.

McCarthy, who joined the team 27 days ago when he was traded from the Minnesota Vikings, had a good day.

He was generally efficient, completing 20 of 28 passes for 252 yards. He didn't throw a touchdown pass, but didn't throw an interception and didn't fumble, either.

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers fired back at NBC's "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker on Sunday over his allegations about Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed and the Muslim Brotherhood, accusing Welker of defending his rival during a heated exchange about the Islamist organization.

Rogers challenged Welker after she said that El-Sayed had already disavowed any ties to the Muslim Brotherhood and defended her previous interview with El-Sayed in which he denied any ties to the group.

"No, he has not, he dismissed the question ... I don't know why you give this guy a pass," Rogers said, as the two interrupted each other. "You are giving him a pass on something he should be accountable for."

MIKE ROGERS PRESSES CNN'S DANA BASH ON WHY THE PRESS IS 'EAGER' TO DEFEND ABDUL EL-SAYED

Welker pressed Rogers on his own 2012 remarks, displaying a past quote where he said the U.S. would have to "reach out to and talk to" moderate members of the Muslim Brotherhood and asking whether he acknowledged having once been willing to engage with them.

Rogers accused Welker of twisting his words to defend El-Sayed rather than scrutinize his opponent's record. He explained that, as House Intelligence Committee chairman at the time, his focus was on preserving intelligence cooperation between Egypt and Israel to prevent further regional violence.

"What you're doing now is trying to twist this thing to defend your position for letting him lie to you," he added.

The confrontation intensified when Welker pressed Rogers about President Donald Trump's characterization of El-Sayed as a violent terrorist. Welker challenged the accusation, saying there was no evidence to support it. She also noted that El-Sayed had denied any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood and publicly disavowed the organization.

Rogers rejected the suggestion that he had personally described his Democratic opponent as a terrorist.

"I've never called him a terrorist," Rogers said.

MICHIGAN SENATE RIVALS CLASH OVER MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD ALLEGATIONS AS ROGERS DOUBLES DOWN ON EL-SAYED

Rogers' campaign doubled down on his criticism in a statement to Fox News Digital, with spokesperson Abby Ronson questioning El-Sayed's responses and urging national media outlets to scrutinize his record.

"Abdul is an Oxford-trained debater," Ronson said. "Yet every time he’s asked about his support of the Muslim Brotherhood, he deflects, gets angry and dismisses the question. Michiganders deserve an answer on what should be an incredibly easy question to answer."

"Why won’t his campaign put out an equivocal [sic] statement disavowing a terrorist organization? The national media should start asking him why that is instead of making excuses for him," she continued.

Rogers' allegations stem from previously reported connections between El-Sayed, members of his family and the Muslim Brotherhood, including a 2012 letter supporting Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood-backed president, Mohamed Morsi.

The Washington Free Beacon reported that El-Sayed was among 46 Egyptian American community figures who signed a November 2012 letter backing Morsi's decisions and urging him to purge Egypt's police and media. Past social media posts from El-Sayed's half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, recently surfaced and described their family's history with the Muslim Brotherhood. In one 2012 post, Abdelhadi acknowledged longstanding family connections to the organization.

In another post, Abdelhadi described a conversation with her mother about participating in Muslim Brotherhood activism while attending college in Egypt during the 1970s.

El-Sayed has maintained that he was raised by his father and stepmother and has accused Rogers of exploiting his Muslim faith for political purposes. Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

He denied that he or his family had ties to the organization when Welker questioned him during an Oct. 11 appearance on "Meet the Press."

World.title: Mary Peltola delays campaign events after sustaining ‘minor injuries’ in car crash
World.content:
Former Rep. Mary Peltola is rescheduling several upcoming campaign events after she and her family sustained “minor” injuries in a car crash, her campaign announced Sunday.

“Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary’s upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover,” Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce said in a statement.

“Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families,” Bruce added.

Peltola was en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives’ annual banquet Saturday when a vehicle transporting the candidate and her family was struck by another driver, according to the campaign. A spokesperson for the campaign said they had no reason to believe the accident had been politically motivated.

The police department in Anchorage confirmed Sunday that a collision involving three vehicles occurred on evening and those involved sustained “non-life threatening injuries.”

Police added that the incident is under investigation.

Peltola, a Democrat, is locked in a competitive Senate race against GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan. She was elected to the House in 2022 but narrowly lost her re-election bid in 2024, the same year that President Donald Trump won the state by 13 percentage points.

Sullivan’s re-election race, in which he’s seeking a third term, is tighter than expected, with Alaska voters tying Trump to high gas and grocery prices resulting from the ongoing war with Iran.

Trump and Vice President JD Vance rallied voters in Alaska separately earlier this month.

Republicans have accused Democrats of recruiting another candidate named Dan Sullivan to run for the Senate, saying that voters may be confused by the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot if they plan to vote for the incumbent senator.

Democrats have not taken credit for recruiting the second Dan Sullivan into the race. He’ll appear on the ballot as Dan J. Sullivan, while the incumbent senator will be identified by his name, political party and a clear notation that he’s the incumbent.

Last week, the Justice Department sued Alaska’s election officials, seeking to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses. It cited Dan J. Sullivan’s presence on the ballot as a point of “voter confusion.”

On Saturday, Democrats filed a motion urging a federal judge to dismiss the case.

World.title: How Democrats could win the House, how the GOP could hang on, and where to look for a wave
World.content:
Districts to watch: NC-14, KY-6

Another way to estimate the possible size of November’s swing is to look at the partisan shifts in elections held in 2025 and 2026, ever since Trump returned to office. These races include the 2025 governor’s elections in New Jersey and Virginia, other high-profile statewide elections and several special elections for the U.S. House.

Although Trump lost Virginia and New Jersey, the other recent elections have tended to occur in places that supported Trump in 2024. Averaging across all of these states and districts, Trump won them by an average of about 3.5 percentage points in 2024. In the 2025 and 2026 elections, however, those states and districts supported the Democratic candidate by an average of about 11 points. This amounts to a shift of 14.5 points in the Democrats’ favor.

If the Democrats are able to shift the vote in every district by such a historically massive margin in 2026, they could win as many as 263 seats to the Republicans’ 172. That would be the largest majority that either party has held in the U.S. House since the 1990 midterm elections.

Such a shift could put into play districts like Florida’s 27th District, represented by GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar. Republicans in Florida left this district nearly unchanged when they redrew the state’s congressional map, believing that a district that Trump won by 14.6 points would be out of reach for the Democrats.

But it appears the race in this heavily Hispanic district is tightening, as polls show Latino voters nationwide turning against Trump and Republicans, with economic concerns weighing heavily on their minds. These voters were critical to Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, and indications that they are moving back toward Democrats are helping drive the party’s competitiveness in Republican-leaning, heavily Hispanic districts in states like Texas, too. Salazar outran Trump’s win margin by nearly 6 percentage points in 2024, and her survival in the 2026 election may require a similarly strong overperformance.

A 14.5-point national swing toward Democrats could also make North Carolina’s 14th District competitive. Republican Rep. Tim Moore’s district is one that North Carolina Republicans did not bother changing when they redrew their maps last year. Trump won the district by 15.1 points, and Moore himself won it in 2024 by 16.1 points.

Another district to watch is Kentucky’s 6th District. Republican Andy Barr has held this open Lexington-based seat since 2013, and Trump carried it in 2024 by 15 points. Barr is running for the U.S. Senate this year. Republican- and Democratic-aligned groups are spending heavily here, reflecting the importance of the race, as Republican Ralph Alvarado faces off against Democrat Zach Dembo.

The NBC News Decision Desk rates this race as lean Republican. In 2024, this district reported almost 90% of its votes by 8:40 p.m. ET. If Democrats are on track for a massive national shift, this district may provide one of the best pieces of early evidence.

National trends don’t mean every district shifts the same amount

To be sure, all of these scenarios assume that the partisan shift in 2026 will be the same in every district. This may be true on average, but some districts will have a larger shift than the national average and others will have a smaller one.

Demographics of a specific district may play a role in the size of the shift. For example, if Hispanic voters shift more dramatically toward the Democratic Party than non-Hispanic voters, then districts with higher concentrations of Hispanic voters will vote more favorably for the Democrats than the underlying partisanship of the district would predict.

Incumbency can also play a large role in causing a district to shift more or less than the national average. In 2024, the incumbent members of Congress outperformed their party’s presidential candidate by an average of 2.5 percentage points.

This year, there are slightly more Democrats seeking re-election than Republican ones. This means that the Democratic Party as a whole stands to gain more from the benefits of incumbency compared with the Republican Party.

On the other hand, there are more Republicans who represent districts with evenly divided underlying partisanship. For example, an “incumbency bump” matters a lot more to a Republican in a district Trump won by 5 points than to a Democrat in a district Harris won by 25 points.

Finally, redistricting has also played a key role in this year’s midterms. By redrawing districts in several states, Republicans stand to win as many as 10 more seats than if the map remained unchanged after 2024.

Redistricting impacts the role of incumbency, too. When the lines for a district are redrawn, incumbents are fighting for the votes of people whom they’ve never represented and who may be less familiar with their records. This tends to diminish the size of the incumbency advantage. Republican incumbents in Texas and other red states and Democratic incumbents in California must lean heavily on the “D” or “R” next to their names when they try to win the support of their new potential constituents.

Former President Barack Obama, appearing in Ohio on Saturday at his first campaign rally of this fall’s midterm elections, called President Donald Trump an agent of “chaos and cruelty” and a man of broken promises.

Obama’s visit was aimed at boosting two Democrats: Amy Acton, the party’s nominee for governor; and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who has mounted a comeback bid for his old job.

Obama was particularly scornful of Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad aimed at Acton, saying there is “no line” Ramaswamy won’t cross.

Later in the night, Obama rallied for Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit. The city, where 75% of the population is Black, is crucial to statewide victories.

Notable quote

Iranian plots to kill U.S. officials have reached ‘advanced stages,’ intel memo warns

Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, on Oct. 19. Kylie Cooper / Pool/AFP via Getty

Iran has stepped up efforts to target U.S. personnel in the Middle East and elsewhere, according to a memo Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Friday.

The memo warned that “the lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages.”

A U.S. official confirmed the memo’s authenticity to NBC News after it was first reported by Axios.

The intelligence comes days after sources told NBC News that the U.S. military has been quietly scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East. The State Department has also ordered further staff reductions at multiple diplomatic posts in the region, including in Lebanon, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Jordan, according to a State Department official.

Clayton told Rubio that the risk was “relevant to more individuals than are currently cleared to receive this information,” adding: “We will make every effort to downgrade as much intelligence as possible so you can share it with State Department personnel at your discretion.”

‘Meet the Press’

Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif., told NBC’s “Meet the Press” that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth should testify before the Senate on the Starlink satellite limitations that disrupted Ukrainian military operations.

If Democrats retake the Senate, Schiff told moderator Kristen Welker, “Defense Secretary Hegseth should be brought in. Anyone who has knowledge of what happened.”

“I’ve never called [El-Sayed] a terrorist,” Rogers said on “Meet the Press” after being asked about Trump’s comments.

Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pushed back on comments made by former first lady Michelle Obama last year that U.S. voters aren’t ready to elect a woman as president.

“Listen, I have got a lot of colleagues who I think are probably interested in running for president, and I’ve heard everyone say, ‘You can’t have this person or that person,’” the governor told “Meet the Press.”

World.title: Inside the controversial call that ended Game 2 of the World Series
World.content:
The Milwaukee Brewers are two wins away from the first World Series title in franchise history, and they got a little help from an incredibly close call Saturday night.

With the Brewers leading 5-4 in the top of the ninth, the Rays had a runner on third with two outs and designated hitter Yandy Díaz at the plate. On a 3-2 pitch that would have been ball four, Díaz tried to check his swing on a curveball from Aaron Ashby.

Home plate umpire Jim Wolf initially ruled that Díaz hadn’t swung, which would have sent him to first base. But Milwaukee catcher William Contreras appealed to the first base umpire, who ruled that Díaz had gone around. The strikeout ended the game.

Here’s how the swing looked in real time:

And here’s how it looked on replay:

“In the moment, yeah, I disagreed. But the umpire said it was a swing and it is what it is,” Díaz said after the game.

“I didn’t go look at it, but from my vantage point, it did look like that he swung,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said.

The postgame crew on the Fox broadcast seemed split over the swing as well.

What exactly is a checked swing?

It’s a great question, and one that MLB’s rulebook doesn’t answer.

According to MLB.com, “there is no definition for ‘check swing’ in the official baseball rules. The closest thing comes in the definition of terms where the first example of a strike is a pitch that ‘is struck at by the batter.’”

That leaves it to the umpires’ discretion when a pitch is considered to be “struck at.”

Colloquially, a batter has to break an imaginary plane for a checked swing to be considered a full one. What exactly is that plane? Again, there’s no official rule. As with obscenity in Jacobellis v. Ohio, umpires typically know it when they see it.

Why didn’t the Rays challenge the call?

Much to the delight of fans, MLB introduced the automated ball-strike (ABS) system this season, allowing players to challenge, as the name suggests, balls and strikes. ABS came on top of the expanded replay review rules instituted in 2014, which granted managers at least one challenge per game on calls such as force plays, tag plays and even fan interference.

Unfortunately for Tampa Bay, checked swings aren’t on the list of reviewable plays, so the Rays couldn’t ask for a review of the play in Game 2.

“We got ABS for the first time this year, getting the balls and strikes right. We need to get a system that can get [checked swings] right,” Fox play-by-play announcer Joe Davis said during a replay of Díaz’s swing.

Will this happen again?

Given all the technology MLB has at its disposal, it’s hard to believe the league and players union will let a situation like Game 2’s happen again, particularly when the stakes are as high as the World Series.

In 2024, MLB tested checked-swing challenges in the Arizona Fall League, using the same Hawk-Eye technology used for the ABS system. In those challenges, teams were able to review if a checked swing “crossed a 45-degree threshold from home plate,” according to MLB.com.

The checked-swing challenge has since made it to the minors, introduced to the single-A Florida State League in 2025 and the Triple-A Pacific Coast League this year.

In June 2025, MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred said he wanted teams to be accustomed to the ABS system before introducing the checked-swing challenge to the majors.

“We haven’t made a decision about the checked-swing thing,” Manfred said at the time. “We do try to think sequentially about what’s coming. I think we got to get over the hump in terms of either doing ABS or not doing it before you’d get into the complication of a separate kind of challenge involved in an at-bat, right? You think about them, they’re two different systems operating at the same time. We really got to think that one through.”

World.title: Kimi Antonelli wins U.S. Grand Prix in Texas, putting him on the brink of F1 championship
World.content:
AUSTIN, Texas — Kimi Antonelli won the U.S. Grand Prix on Sunday with a dominant lights-to-flag drive, putting him on the brink of becoming the 2026 Formula 1 world champion.

The 20-year-old Mercedes driver fell just short of clinching the title in Texas, but he extended his already commanding lead and is on the verge of making history as F1’s youngest-ever champion in just his second season.

The Italian has an excellent opportunity to lock down the title at the Mexico City race next Sunday.

It was a masterful drive from Antonelli, who proved once again why he’s cruising to a world championship. James Sutton / LAT Images via Getty

Antonelli on Sunday came closer to being the first Italian to win the world championship since Alberto Ascari in 1953. Clive Rose / Getty

With five races to go, Antonelli sits 124 points ahead of his nearest rival with a maximum of 125 points up for grabs. The race in Austin marked his ninth victory of the season.

“It was the result we needed,” Antonelli said in a post-race interview. “We’re very close, but yeah, we trying to finish on a high and hopefully we can finish it very soon.”

Behind Antonelli, Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc finished second and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen finished third. Neither is in contention for the title. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton finished fourth. And George Russell, also with Mercedes, finished eighth, barely staying in mathematical contention in the standings.

Even before the Austin race, Russell and Hamilton both spoke of Antonelli securing the 2026 title as a matter of when, not if.

Antonelli would break a record set by 23-year-old Sebastian Vettel, who won the trophy in a title-deciding thriller at the final race of the 2010 F1 season. Antonelli was four years old at the time and joked to NBC News that he recalls playing with Hot Wheels.

He would also become the first Italian to win the world championship since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

F1 officials counted an attendance of 467,000 this weekend.

It was a masterful drive from Antonelli, who proved once again why he’s cruising to a world championship. He started first on Sunday and sped off into the distance as Verstappen battled with the two Ferraris in the opening laps.

Antonelli pitted on Lap 25 of 56 for his one and only stop to change tires. Leclerc and Verstappen both sought two-stop strategies to try and catch him, but failed to do so. Leclerc overtook Verstappen in the final stint of the race.

And it was another weekend in which Russell, 28, was one step behind his younger teammate and rival when it counted. Russell qualified sixth and held that position in the opening stages of the race. But on Lap 9, Russell was given a 5-second time penalty for “leaving the track and gaining an advantage,” which cost him positions and eventually dropped him to eighth.

World.title: Brazil counts votes in presidential runoff between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro
World.content:
Vote-counting resumed in Brazil's polarizing presidential runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro after voting hours were extended following requests by both candidates for an extension based on issues with voting in their respective strongholds.

The extension had caused confusion at many polling stations. Some had already shut down when the decision — made by a Supreme Court justice three minutes before poll close time — was relayed to them several minutes after they'd already shut down, and results were paused until the end of the two-hour window.

The decision set the stage for possible legal challenges no matter who wins. Lula's camp said it was already looking into taking legal action because of "interference in the electoral process," said Edhinho Silva, chairman of Lula's Workers Party.

Bolsonaro's campaign had yet to comment. Bolsonaro ally Nikolas Ferreira is saying the decision that came from the Supreme Court justice, who is also Lula's ex-lawyer, is an attempt to contest Bolsonaro's likely win.

The contest will determine whether the U.S. will significantly expand its growing influence in Latin America. A win for Bolsonaro would signify a pivot to the right by Latin America's most populous country and its largest economy, in a year when Trump allies have scored victories in Chile, Peru and Colombia. A victory for Lula would leave Brazil and Mexico with left-of-center leaders.

Polls showed the two candidates, who need more than 50% of the vote to become Brazil's next leader in January, in a neck-and-neck race. The election pits the left-of-center veteran politician Lula against Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump and the son of imprisoned former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro.

Voters line up at a polling station during the presidential runoff in Brasilia, Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Eraldo Peres

Judge rules to extend voting by 2 hours

As polls were closing, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin ruled to extend voting nationwide for two hours. The ruling came after both presidential candidates had asked the electoral court to extend voting hours in some cities.

Lula's request came after issues in nine states with buses that provide transportation to polls. Bolsonaro's request was due to heavy rains in Brazil's south.

In Brasilia, volunteers who oversaw the vote count at a school debated whether they needed to stay after the announcement to extend voting, but most left 15 to 20 minutes after polls closed and they had given count information to electoral authorities.

Bolsonaro bested Lula by more than 2.2 million votes in the first round of the election earlier this month. However, more than 33 million voters out of nearly 160 million did not turn out.

Bolsonaro and Lula have opposing ideological views on issues ranging from U.S.-Brazil relations and climate change to social welfare.

In many ways, Brazil's runoff vote is another tight rematch between the country's two polarized political forces that trigger passion as much as loathing. Four years ago, Lula beat Bolsonaro's father by the narrowest margin since the country's return to democracy in 1985.

Security and cost-of-living concerns

Lula, who first governed Brazil between 2003 and 2010, has faced a tough reelection battle because of concerns about the cost of living and security. Bolsonaro made a tough-on-crime approach the cornerstone of his campaign and pledged to bring down food costs.

Both have been hit by corruption suspicions involving family members and allies, with Bolsonaro implicated in a sprawling scandal rocking Brazil. Lula previously spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were eventually annulled.

Bolsonaro's admission that he accepted about $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.

Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro and his wife Fernanda Bolsonaro give a thumbs during the runoff presidential election in Rio de Janeiro, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Silvia Izuierdo

As Bolsonaro voted at a school in Rio de Janeiro, his supporters shouted "Lula, thief, your place is in prison" while Lula's supporters chanted in his support.

"The time of real change has arrived," Bolsonaro said. "Brazil can't go on for another four years on its current trajectory."

In the lead-up to the vote, Lula frequently portrayed Bolsonaro, whose father is under house arrest for attempting a coup, as a threat to democracy. Bolsonaro has promised to seek an amnesty for his father if elected.

Lula, trying to lure undecided voters, has invested in costly incentives. His government endorsed a debt relief program for small businesses and promised free public transportation on weekends. A major win then came when the Senate backed a popular proposal to end the six-day working week.

Lula thanked his voters for an outpouring of support while casting his ballot in the city of Sao Bernardo do Campo, where he began his political career as a union leader in the 1960s. "It is a lot of generosity, a lot of care, a lot of love. I will be forever grateful," Lula said.

Lula voters respect his past; Bolsonaro voters want change

Lula voters turned out Sunday driven by his history of supporting marginalized people and working to lift Brazilians out of poverty.

"Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it's like to be poor," Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in Rio de Janeiro, said. "I find it impossible not to vote for him."

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who is seeking reelection, waves after voting in the presidential runoff in Sao Bernardo do Campo, Brazil, Sunday, Oct. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Andre Penner

Anderson Falcão, a 43-year-old journalist in Brasilia who sported a red shirt in support of Lula, said he worried about Bolsonaro's long-term political vision, which he called "exclusionary."

"It's a project that harms the less fortunate, harms the worker, women, the forest, the Amazon," he said.

Bolsonaro voters, many of whom wore yellow and green Brazil jerseys in support of the senator, said they want change.

"Things are really expensive and taxes are too high," Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist in Rio de Janeiro, said. She added that she once voted for Lula's party but now associates it with corruption.

Third-party voters and abstentions from first round could decide vote

Kelvin Gomes Pimental, a 28-year-old data analyst in Brasilia, voted for a third-party candidate in the first round, making his vote a decisive one in this election. He ultimately decided to vote for Lula.

"It's not even about Flávio himself. It's also very much about the management of the other Bolsonaro government. He wanted to stage a coup," he said. "These issues scare me a little."

Diogo Furtado, a 35-year-old Uber driver in Rio de Janeiro, didn't vote the first time because of his work, but said he'll vote blank on Sunday. He said that neither candidate convinced him.

"Brazil needs a new candidate," Furtado said. "But unfortunately our country has become dominated by two names: Lula and Bolsonaro."

Issues with public transportation affect the vote

In Bahia state, a stronghold for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose voters tend to live in areas that depend more heavily on buses, at least 75 public buses were prevented from leaving municipal garages during the presidential runoff vote, according to a state electoral judge. He ordered the arrest of the mobility secretary of the capital, Salvador, Pablo Souza, in relation to the case.

Mayor Bruno Reis, a Bolsonaro ally, blamed trade unionists for illegally sticking Workers' Party materials onto transit vehicles for the measure.

President of Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, confirmed that electoral authorities received a report on problems with buses in Bahia that is being analyzed. He did not confirm if voting would be extended, which Lula requested in Salvador and Sao Paulo, where issues with public transportation were also reported in the city with a mayor allied with Bolsonaro.

"We will not be robbed by mayors, governors or businessmen," Lula told the press. "These people need to respect democracy."

Bolsonaro did not immediately comment on the issue.

International observers earlier in the day said that voting was occurring peacefully and with transparency and did not immediately comment on the incident.

The Trump administration looms large

Lula criticized the U.S. president before Brazil's election, speaking about the risks of U.S. intervention in Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports and classified drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations. Experts say the moves may have been intended to make Lula look soft on crime.

Flávio Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House and insisted that Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including in the rare minerals economy. Brazil estimates that its deposits hold up to 21 million tons, second only to China. He denies he's being helped by the U.S. government.

Mr. Trump said Sunday that he is watching the election but declined to endorse a candidate.

Voting in Brazil is conducted electronically and the result is usually available within hours after polling stations close at 5 p.m. in Brasilia.

World.title: Vucic concedes defeat in Serbia's parliamentary election
World.content:
The long-serving strongman leader of Serbia, Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat on Sunday in an election that pitted him and his right-wing party against a diverse student-led opposition movement that spent two years protesting his government.

It was a seismic political shift in the Balkan country where Vucic, who had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin and who denounced the student movement as a foreign-led attempt to unseat him, led with virtually absolute power for 14 years.

High turnout and gathering tensions marked the highly contested parliamentary election that was a showdown between Vucic and his right-wing Serbian Progressive Party and university students who, accusing the government of corruption and dismantling democracy, had built a popular following across the country.

Serbia's 6.4 million voters were electing lawmakers to the 250-member Parliament. In conceding the election, Vucic said his party projects that his opponents, the youth-backed Students' List, will take between 135 and 140 seats while his SNS party will have around 105.

"The Students' List has won," Vucic told supporters at his party's election night event, though he blamed Serbia's independent media as well as alleged interference by unnamed European countries and an "American deep state" for the loss.

Aleksandar Vucic casts his ballot at a polling station in a school in Belgrade, Serbia, on October 25, 2026, during the country's early parliamentary elections. Samir Jordamovic/Anadolu via Getty Images

Vucic said that his SNS party won around 1.7 million votes compared to the Students' List, which he said took around 2.2 million.

Supporters of the Students' List immediately flooded onto the streets of Belgrade and other cities, honking horns, shouting and chanting: "Aleksandar is gone," referring to Vucic.

The outcome, which Vucic announced only around an hour and a half after polls closed, came after tensions had built as voting progressed during the day.

Police in anti-riot gear cordoned off an area in central Belgrade around the election commission headquarters. Special police vehicles could be seen near a Belgrade park where Vucic's loyalists have been camping for over a year, and large groups of black-clad men had congregated at various points throughout the city.

Vucic was seeking to become Serbia's prime minister after serving two near-full terms as president. He resigned the presidency last month to lead the campaign.

Support for the populist had eroded since 16 people were killed in 2024 when a concrete canopy collapsed at a train station in Novi Sad. That set off a wave of youth protests that blamed the collapse on high-level corruption, cronyism and rampant graft during renovation work at the station.

Despite the protests, Vucic retained considerable support among many of Serbia's voters. Admirers viewed him as a capable leader who can steer the nation through global uncertainties - the image that was carefully crafted by the mainstream media.

While the increasingly authoritarian Vucic has routinely outplayed Serbia's fractured opposition in the past, the leaderless youth movement proved to be a tough opponent that rattled his firm grip on power in Serbia like no one else in the 14 years since his party took office.

The newly formed Students' List movement was shaped by university students, but none actually appeared on the election list. Instead, its candidates are little-known experts, athletes, farmers and artists.

This approach was meant to counter Vucic's one-man rule and restore a sense of community and solidarity. The students' message during the campaign focused on a non-partisan effort to rebuild Serbia's economy and restore its democracy.
