World.title: Mezcal production, Mother Earth and the enduring spirit of the Zapotecs
World.content:
Nestled between the Pan-American Highway and the Rio Grande, all along the Ruta Caminos del Mezcal, exist hundreds of palenques, or small farms that carry the ancient practice of mezcal production. Tourists come in droves to watch the mules pull the great stone wheel of the tahona in slow circles, crushing roasted agave before it is fermented, distilled and enjoyed.

I had the pleasure of learning about this age-old practice firsthand, a practice that existed long before it became a spectacle for curious travelers, while living and volunteering at one of these fabled farms.

How community and ecology sustain mezcal production

The land once belonged to the Zapotecs, an ancient civilization known for its profound connection to the natural and spiritual worlds. Inhabiting the land for more than 2,500 years, the Zapotecs were first overtaken by the Aztecs beginning in the late 15th century, and subsequently by the infamous Spanish conquistador Hernán Cortés.

Although the group suffered decimation from disease and invasion, around 500,000 Zapotec speakers remain in the Oaxaca region. That air of tradition survives in the people and culture of Oaxaca today: in the emphasis on community, in farming and ecological initiatives, in spiritual practice and myth, and most notably, in mezcal.

Oaxaca, the mezcal capital of the world, is also known for its ecological initiatives and Earth-centered culture, and remains a place of continual education and philosophy for anyone passionate about a lifestyle that benefits the planet.

Indigenous and mestizo communities own nearly 82% of the state’s 6.1 million hectares of forest, managing them collectively rather than as private property. Zapotec is still spoken in several municipalities, and local mythology and spiritually driven land stewardship make the state an example of an ecologically sustainable community.

First sip goes to the Earth and ancestors

In Zapotec tradition, mezcal brings people closer to the spirits. Across Oaxaca, it is common to pour the first sip for the thirsty earth and for ancestors long gone.

As the glasses are raised and the offering given, participants speak the word “Dixeebe” over the anointed ground. Dixeebe is a Zapotec salutation used to express deep reverence for the spirit of Earth. The gesture is small, but it is a daily reminder to put the needs of the Earth, and of those no longer living on it, before one’s own. Repeated across a community, it builds a culture devoted to a better planet for all of us.

This inherent reverence and respect for the Earth reverberates through small, traditional mezcal-producing palenques across the Oaxacan region.

1 of 13

Protecting the land is protecting mezcal

For Miguel Ángel Zamora, mezcal maestro at Casa Cabrón in Unión Zapata, protecting the land and protecting mezcal are inextricably linked. Casa Cabrón is one of many family-run palenques in Unión Zapata that remain true to the traditional culture of mezcal production.

Regarding his production process, Zamora says, “That connection (to the Earth) is so important for life in general, and can also be achieved through mezcal. But first, we must be conscious of producing it in a conscious way.”

He goes on to say, “We must care for Mother Earth, because from her flows the medicine that heals our soul, mind, body and life.”

‘Revealing a bit of life’s magic’

The mezcal production process begins on monthly cycles.

During harvest day, jimadores use machetes to cut and carve the agave plants’ core and prepare them for pickup. After the batch is cut and ready, workers from the palenque or neighboring farms retrieve the haul from the mountains and bring it back to the palenques for production.

“For me, producing mezcal means revealing a bit of life’s magic, the magic of transformation,” Zamora says. “It means showing the world that processes rooted in great love and respect for Mother Earth foster life, enjoyment, bliss and joy.”

The following day the crew and I headed back to the harvesting site promptly at 4:45 a.m. to pick up the agave and deliver it. The trip to the Sierra Mixe mountains was a generous three hours, even with our skilled, quick driver.

As we maneuvered the mountains’ impressive turns, the men talked of the prior night’s full moon, healthy horses and newly bought motorcycles. My traveling companions would point out edible plants, dangerous cacti or friends’ palenques, all the while passing snacks over my shoulder.

Once we arrived at the agave harvesting site, beverages were shared over small coolers, while the workers formed assembly lines — one man lifted the cut-down plant, tossed it to the next, and finally threw it into the back of the exporting truck.

Despite the physically demanding work and intense heat, there was no shortage of laughter. It was easy to mistake our hard work for a friendly reunion.

Navigating the tradition-modernity divide

Although larger mezcal corporations have pitched their tent along the mezcal route in recent years, family-run mezcal farms remain, with their beliefs intact and traditions upheld. Contrasts between old and new, nature and machines, are everywhere in Oaxaca. Local ruins exist amongst modern towns. Spanish churches are built upon ancient Zapotec temples.

Nowhere is this divide clearer than at the Church of San Pablo in Mitla. An ancient Zapotec ceremonial site, this once-great temple was torn down and rebuilt by Spanish Dominican friars, turning the structure into a Catholic institution. However, the original Zapotec foundations remain, creating a haunting visual representation of religious syncretism within the region and the enduring Indigenous presence.

As I walked through the ruins, our guide, a local Zapotec historian and teacher, led us past fallen walls and shrunken tombs that once sheltered a people defined by their relationship to the natural world. Spirals of life and death decorated the low-hanging frames, and old women passed, the numinous melody of the Zapotec language drifting in their wake.

We had brought our guide freshly distilled mezcal to taste, and he insisted we pour the first sip for the thirsty ground and the ancestors. We stood together, surrounded by the imposing walls of the temple’s spiritual resilience, and poured the first sip of mezcal onto the ancient stone floors.

We saluted using the Zapotec word dixeebe, while remembering all those who had been at this very spot before us.

The Zapotec civilization may have been nearly lost to time, but its beliefs and the spirit of its people live on in Oaxaca and, evidently, around the world, carried in the smoky, sultry, handmade spirit of mezcal.

Abigail Rose is a journalist, archaeologist and storyteller with a hands-on, in-the-field approach to journalism. She reports on local environmental initiatives, cultural stories and frontline conflict through writing, photography and video. Her work has taken her across Colombia, Peru, Oman, Greece, Mexico, Ecuador, Germany, Italy and the U.S., with her next project bringing her to Oaxaca, Mexico.

World.title: Mexico Well-Read: A review of Sofía Robleda’s ‘The Other Moctezuma Girls’
World.content:
Anyone who has stood in Mexico City’s Zócalo has felt the weight of history; beneath the cathedral and the crowds lie Tenochtitlán and the blood and bones of conquest. The city has spent the succeeding five centuries deciding which parts of that story to tell. The usual cast is familiar: Moctezuma, Cortés, Cuauhtémoc and a Malinche as contested now as she was in 1519.

Rarely, however, does anyone linger on Tecuichpoch, Moctezuma’s favored daughter, baptized Isabel. She was consort to two Mexica emperors, Cuitláhuac and Cuauhtémoc, bore a daughter to Cortés, and later married three other Spaniards. Her life ran through nearly every famous name of the Conquest, yet she barely registers in the popular telling.

‘A disturbing tapestry’

Robleda decided to address that lack in her new novel, “The Other Moctezuma Girls,” an ambitious, often moving romp across history and the fascinating cultural geography of the Valley of Mexico.

The story opens in Tenochtitlán in 1551, 30 years after the Spanish Conquest, as Tecuichpoch’s will is read aloud after her death. Her daughter Isabel suspects that a second account of her mother’s life may be hidden, chapter by chapter. The clues to that inheritance are found in a disturbing tapestry bequeathed to Isabel and her younger sister in the will. Isabel sets out to follow them with her favorite siblings and a handsome young cook.

Alongside Isabel’s journey runs her mother’s own testimony, delivered in the first person by a woman who knows her time is short:

“Moctezuma, Cuauhtemoc, Cortés, Malintzin … they reshaped the order of the entire world. They may be dead, but by God, they are known. Yet no one but you will know me. I may be mentioned in passing as the child, the wife, the mistress … Listen to me, rambling on. Trying to carve out a pinprick of light in the darkness these people have cast over my life. It is very difficult, for I was also taught not to exalt myself, not to seek attention, lest I be judged, or mocked, or worse, publicly shamed. As my mother would say, Tlacoqualli in monequi — moderation is a must.”

Nearing death, Tecuichpoch wants to be known; she declares that she will not die silent. In a line that could serve as the book’s thesis, she observes that “men would leave us nameless, if they could.” That premise gives the novel real moral force.

‘Pure adventure’

Tecuichpoch recalls being married off three times by the age of 12. She was raised, as Nahua women of the age were, to keep her face serene, and she credits that discipline with her survival. The empress describes her father’s love as a weapon that cut both ways: She was Moctezuma’s cherished child, and he still handed her to his enemies. Yet she insists he was neither fool nor coward, and that he read the Spanish correctly, as men rather than gods, and as the vanguard of an innumerable and therefore unstoppable horde. It is a humane portrait, and it lets Moctezuma be a father without excusing him.

The domestic details do much of the work. There is the tank of axolotls that Tecuichpoch kept in her father’s zoo, the pranks she played on her father’s other wives, and the beloved brother who collected obsidian and volcanic stones in a wooden box. Anyone who has wandered the Museo Nacional de Antropología will understand why these touches matter. The Mexica are usually presented as a catalog of gods, glyphs and sacrifices, while here they are real people with siblings, grudges and favorite pets. Tecuichpoch’s prose is formal and lightly ornate, sprinkled with Nahuatl as well as Spanish.

Her daughter’s half of the book is more conventional but livelier. One of Isabel’s siblings, Catina, lost her hearing after an illness, and the siblings communicate through sign language, a welcome touch that keeps the teens from becoming a mere chorus of clue-solvers. The quest itself is pure adventure. It takes the young people through the viceregal court and then the chinampas of Xochimilco, into tunnels beneath the ancient pyramids of Teotihuacán, and even up the icy slopes of Iztaccíhuatl as nearby Popocatépetl threatens to erupt.

A highly entertaining mix of history and drama

Since Robleda is writing about a woman forced to live in two worlds at once, it is fitting that the book itself straddles these two modes. While guiding us through an exciting adventure — a deadly scavenger hunt — she also provides fascinating historical information about the colonial caste system, constraints on women, slavery and the lasting consequences of conquest. The country’s mestizo identity, after all, began in the negotiations, marriages and coercions that Tecuichpoch lived through.

Robleda assigns a high degree of respect to la Malinche, or Malintzin, from Tecuichpoch, who is said to have admired her spirit, her brilliance, and the long game this noblewoman-turned-slave-turned-noblewoman managed to play:

“(Malintzin), too, had been reshaped. Cortés had married her off to another of his captains, Juan Jaramillo, and she was no longer a slave but a free noblewoman again. This is what she had desired most in the whole world. Freedom for herself and her children—the young son she’d had with Cortés and Jaramillo’s newborn girl in her arms, who were now peers of the New World aristocracy.”

“The Other Moctezuma Girls” is not a scholarly reckoning, and it does not pretend to be. It is a novel of reclamation, intent on sharing the story of this utterly fascinating woman, the last Mexica empress. It is best suited to readers who enjoy their history with a mystery, a map and a pounding pulse. Take it with you on your next visit to Mexico City, and you may find yourself absorbing the history around you more energetically.

Ann Marie Jackson is a book editor and the award-winning author of “The Broken Hummingbird.” She lives in San Miguel de Allende and can be reached through her website: annmariejacksonauthor.com.

World.title: MND Tutor | Afro-Mexican celebration
World.content:
Welcome to MND Tutor! This interactive learning tool helps you improve your Spanish by exploring real news articles from Mexico News Daily. Instead of just memorizing vocabulary lists or grammar rules, you’ll dive into authentic stories about Mexican culture, current events and daily news.

Oaxaca held its first Afro Guelaguetza in the coastal community of Chacahua Isla, bringing together 12 delegations to celebrate Afro-Mexican heritage through music, masked dances and traditional performances. The festival, known as La Rejunjuneada, gave Afro-Mexican communities a dedicated platform to showcase their cultural traditions, which also feature in the state’s larger annual Guelaguetza celebration. World.title: Full speed ahead: The 39th Carrera Panamericana lives up to its billing
World.content:
“Mexico is the only place in the world where you can pass the police while going 180 mph, and they’ll smile and wave at you,” said Jan Bednar, a professional race car driver who made his debut in Mexico. “I love it. I’m having the best time.”

A few days prior, Bednar had arrived in Mexico from Czechia to compete in the legendary La Carrera Panamericana, or the Pan-American Race.

The Czech driver brought a restored 1969 BMW 3.0 CS that once competed in the Pan-Am over a decade ago. He even gathered the original team that had once raced in Mexico with the same vehicle — a classic German speedster that he said he found collecting dust in a forlorn garage in Eastern Europe. He was inspired when, after asking around, he found out about its former days in the Pan-Am.

Bednar was one of many international motorists from 15 countries to have saved up enough resources — upwards of $75,000 — to race in the 39th edition of La Carrera Panamericana.

A deadly origin story on the open highway

The race has developed a notorious reputation as one of the most dangerous, even deadly, open-road endurance rallies in the world. It launched in 1950 as part of an initiative from the Mexican government to highlight its completion of the Pan-American Highway.

The highway itself, which spans 19,000 miles, was proposed by the United States as a railroad in 1889. In 1923, that idea evolved into an automobile thoroughfare and was revisited at the International Conference of American States in Santiago, Chile.

It took 13 years for the 21 involved nations to sign on to build their respective sections, a sprawling agreement finalized at the Convention on the Pan-American Highway in Buenos Aires, Argentina.

In 1936, the highway — heralded as an international diplomatic success — announced the completion of its first section from Laredo, Texas, to Mexico City. Eventually, Mexico became the first country to finish its border-to-border commitment, prompting the idea for the inaugural Pan-Am race.

The race has since had a controversial, albeit exhilarating, history that brings professional racers, amateurs and hobbyists to Mexico for the landmark event. Known for its high death toll, with more than 30 fatalities in the first five years of its existence, the race was canceled in 1955 and remained dormant until 1988, when it returned in a modernized and regulated format.

A modern course winding through mountain passes

Today, the course extends from Chiapas to Chihuahua, covering eight states and nearly 2,400 miles for a seven-day haul across Mexico’s public roads. It is sectioned into timed portions and various classifications.

While Mexican road conditions have significantly improved since the 1950s, the race is still seen as a perilous task and offers a highly coveted trophy.

After kicking off on Friday, Oct. 16, in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, the 50 registered crews and their vehicles — mostly vintage Porsches, Fords, Studebakers and Chevrolets — flock northward along the coast of Veracruz and up to the state’s port city before banking inland and ascending up the rainy highway into the Sierra Madre mountains toward Puebla.

The 100 drivers made a colorful pit stop in Xalapa, where hundreds of local fans gathered in the parking lot of a science museum to cheer on the competitors, who drove through the city’s avenues as a caravan. Many drivers got out to mingle with supporters and took a smoke break before blazing off in an impressive procession of throttling engines.

The loudest applause came when Xalapa’s first local team, Don Justo, made its anticipated debut. Its two Mexican drivers, Iván Martínez and Salvador Aburto, received a hero’s welcome on their home turf.

Local fandom and international drivers unite

Fans of all ages gathered to witness La Carrera Panamericana in person, which has only passed through Veracruz a handful of times because the route continuously shifts with each edition.

“Motorsports have had a major boom in Mexico since Checo Pérez (debuted in Formula One in 2013),” said Arturo Ibáñez Gómez, a fan from Xalapa. “But it’s not common to always see these racers up close, especially in smaller cities.”

Despite a busy work schedule, Ibáñez Gómez said he wouldn’t miss the rare chance to see the race cars up close, even braving the scattered rain and high winds that morning.

He certainly wasn’t alone in his dedicated fandom. Ramsés López and his father, Alejandro, were in attendance among hundreds of others as car enthusiasts and vintage collectors. For them, having the race in their hometown was a blessing.

For others, being in Xalapa — let alone Mexico — was an unlikely yet thrilling moment. Carter Fournier of Dallas, Texas, entered the race with his 1970 Porsche 911. Like many participants, it was his first time racing south of the U.S. border.

“This is the last road race like this of its kind in the world. It’s special,” Fournier said. “There’s nothing like it left. This is the best of the best. It doesn’t get any better.”

A timeless tradition in North American racing

Notable racers included former Production World Rally Championship champion Benito Guerra Jr., a Mexican legend who was swarmed by fans in his 1983 Porsche 911. His small but muscular car was tailored with RSR specs built specifically for tarmac rally racing.

Though the race has lost some of its universal fame over the decades, it still evokes a sense of romantic timelessness from a renegade era of Mexican motorsports.

For those in the know, it’s a holy grail event in North American racing lore — and worth standing around in inclement weather as part of a large crowd just to give a driver a thumbs-up (trust me, they’ll always give you one back).

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: From the archive: What’s inside that piñata? A guide to Mexican candy
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in June 2025 — is a humorous yet informative look at the candies waiting to be liberated inside Mexico’s iconic piñatas.

If you’ve been in Mexico for a while, chances are you’ve been invited to — and perhaps attended — a few children’s parties.

Whether or not you know the child being celebrated is truly irrelevant. A party is something their parents throw, and they get a big say in who attends. This is only right because parties are expensive.

Sure, at least some of the kid’s friends will be there too. But you’d be forgiven for peeking into a salón de fiesta and wondering why a bunch of beer-drinking grown-ups rented a bouncy house.

A central feature of the Mexican kid’s party — and Christmas party, and New Year’s party — is, of course, the piñata.

Piñatas, as you might guess, have been around for quite a while. Before the papier-mâché varieties of today, for example, piñatas were literally clay pots. (For an informative read on the history of piñatas, check out MND’s excellent article on the subject.)

As a parent, I have watched as my daughter and other guests take turns trying to smash many a piñata to smithereens. My voice has gone hoarse from singing the “dale dale” song; thankfully, I usually have a beer to soothe it. And of course, my heart has stopped many times as I watched particularly enthusiastic children swing with all their might, even as others rushed toward them, one or two pieces of candy on the ground already.

Piñata candy-collecting is not a sport for the weak. You either rush in there and scoop up candy as fast as you can — or you don’t get candy. My daughter, whom I’ve infected with some of my gringa sensibilities, tends to hang back and grab stragglers, often sharing with smaller kids. This is kind, yes, but it’s also safe: She knows she’ll get a gift bag at the end of the party too. Under no circumstances will she go without.

You might think that once your kids get candy, you’ll get candy. This is true. There’s usually plenty to go around, along with — thank goodness — a big supply of local dentists.

Some of the candy is what we’re already familiar with, like chocolate. There are paletas (suckers) too, of course, and the little pieces of hard candy called caramelos.

But, oh, the variety. Everyone seems to love these things around here, so let’s have a look at what some of the less-familiar ones are!

Miguelitos

I have not met a Mexican who does not love miguelitos. My daughter loves them too. I, myself, would rather eat paint chips.

What are miguelitos, you may ask? Well, they’re little paper or plastic packets of powder that, since they’re sold as candy, you would think would be sweet. Basically, it’s a chamoy-flavored powder.

And what is chamoy, you may ask? It’s the stuff on the rim of your glass if you have a michelada, for one. It’s sweet, sour, salty and spicy all at the same time, and Mexicans go nuts for it. In powder or sauce, it goes on fruit, candy, popcorn, the rims of glasses or straight into the mouth. For a fascinating history of chamoy in Mexico, check out this video.

Pelón Pelo Rico

This is another favorite of pretty much every kid I know, including my daughter, and is in the tamarind candy category. Its presentation is silly: it’s a push-up goo made to look like a little green fellow’s red hair. It’s tangy and spicy, and also a little … salty? Not my bag, but it doesn’t have to be: It’s got tons of fans.

Tamarind is the featured flavor in a few other popular Mexican candies as well, like Pulparindo, which my partner calls his personal favorite. This one is just a bit heavier on the spiciness and saltiness — and it’s chewy, like a fruit roll-up. Salty fruit roll-ups, anyone? There’s also a kind of tamarind pulp sold in an actual plastic spoon to lick off!

Mazapán

Now that we’ve talked about some of the many things they put salt and chile in, let’s move on to something, in my opinion, much tastier. Mazapán — De la Rosa is the brand — is a round disk of ground peanuts and sugar pressed together. It’s technically a solid, but it has a way of both breaking off and then melting in your mouth that’s just so satisfying.

Obleas

I was very confused the first time someone handed me one of these. “Are these two body-of-Christ wafers with caramel in the middle?” That’s exactly what they are.

The cream in the middle is cajeta, a gooey caramel made from goat’s milk (the similar dulce de leche is made from cow’s milk). There are also cajeta suckers, which are delicious, and rollos de guayaba filled with cajeta, which are also worth seeking out, though they can’t typically be found in a piñata. I just wanted to mention them because I love them.

Paleta payaso

If you’re lucky, there will be a few of these in the piñata. The paleta payaso is a chocolate-covered marshmallow on a stick with a candied smiley face.

Unwrapping one is always a comical event, because the face is always misshapen. I remember frowning for a good five seconds the first time someone handed me one. But it’s pretty good.

Which Mexican candies do you like?

This article isn’t a complete list — obviously. I tried to stick mostly to things that might seem foreign to … well, foreigners.

Even after 23 years, there are some of these candies that I just don’t like: chile and salt with sweet and sour, for example, will never be okay in my book. But most candies, I do like.

So come on, out with it: What are your Mexican faves?

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Trade optimism holds despite a CIA-linked treason case
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico and the United States were “very close” to a trade deal, both presidents said this week — but lower tariffs were still a negotiating goal, not an agreement. Meanwhile, the arrest of Chihuahua’s former attorney general over alleged unauthorized CIA involvement in a drug raid sharpened the dispute over foreign agents operating in Mexico.

At home, Sheinbaum acknowledged that fuel seized in a much-publicized bust was not stolen, while Guadalajara residents continued to march for clean water. Water is on the mind of many outside Jalisco as well, as recent rains have proven insufficient to ease drought across areas of the country. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Tariff talks and sovereignty

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said Monday that Mexico hoped for U.S. tariff reductions before year-end. Steel and aluminum face 50% duties, while vehicle tariffs include exemptions for U.S. content. USMCA remains in effect despite Washington’s July decision not to extend it another 16 years.

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum outlined the remaining obstacles to a trade agreement: Washington was offering tariff reductions in exchange for concessions Mexico had not fully accepted. She said Mexico would not accept terms that run contrary to its laws or that damage the economy or jobs.

Meanwhile, former Chihuahua Attorney General César Jáuregui was arrested for treason over allegations he authorized CIA participation in an April drug-lab raid without federal approval. On Friday, Sheinbaum recounted how Chihuahua Gov. Maru Campos denied authorizing foreign agents, accusing Jáuregui during a tense private meeting in September.

Mexico also announced plans to file a complaint over Emiliano Andrade Covarrubias’ death in ICE custody. The Foreign Ministry counted 18 Mexican deaths in custody or during immigration operations since Trump’s second term began. At the same time, U.S. authorization to test a heat ray along the Mexico-U.S. border raised concerns about possible burn injuries to targets on both sides of the border.

Security claims under scrutiny

On Tuesday, the U.N. Committee on Enforced Disappearances’ chairman urged General Assembly consideration of Mexico’s disappearances crisis. Mexico rejects the committee’s crimes-against-humanity characterization.

Wednesday brought official figures of 2,539 fuel-related arrests since October 2024, but also a qualification: Sheinbaum said 59 million liters confiscated in Guanajuato were not stolen or illegally imported. The company from which the fuel was confiscated had produced documentation establishing the facility’s legal operation, while the federal prosecutor in Guanajuato was fired and placed under investigation over irregularities in the bust.

Friday’s urban security survey found 58.1% of adults in surveyed cities felt unsafe, the lowest proportion in the series begun in 2013.

Water protests and persistent drought

Guadalajara’s contaminated-water crisis drew another mass protest a week after a similar protest ended with arrests and accusations of police brutality. This past Sunday, some 10,000 people marched. Participants blamed masked infiltrators for violence along the route, but their affiliations remained unestablished. Residents’ demands for clean tap water remained unresolved.

Nationally, rainfall had not erased accumulated drought deficits. Moderate-to-severe drought covered 12.7% of Mexico on Oct. 15, compared with 7.5% a year earlier. Rain helped some northern areas but failed to reverse earlier shortfalls in the south and southeast.

Economy and labor

The peso closed Thursday at 18.71 per dollar, depreciating 9.7% since Sept. 4. A narrower Mexico-U.S. interest-rate gap and trade uncertainty contributed to the slide.

Also on Thursday, the government announced 20 additional industrial parks, bringing Plan México’s operating total to 40.

In labor news, healthcare workers’ protests appear to be winding down after the union representing IMSS workers negotiated a new pay agreement. The package combines 4% more base pay with 4% in housing assistance, below the requested 10% base-pay increase; demonstrators also demanded medicines and better conditions. While protesters have promised to keep pressing for a better deal, attendance at the most recent marches dwindled following the improved pay offer.

Healthcare was not the only public service under examination: MND’s education deep dive found that more young adults are completing upper secondary education, even as education spending as a share of GDP and student test scores declined over the periods reviewed.

Politics and legislation

The Morena party’s dominance in Mexican politics appears to be holding strong, with early polling showing Morena as the overwhelming favorite in next year’s 2027 midterm elections. The party is preferred by 46% of Mexicans, although 31% expressed no preference and party preferences for gubernatorial contests were more varied.

Senators approved legislation that would allow the Finance Ministry to require digital payments in designated sectors, with gas stations and highway tollbooths expected to be among the first affected. Supporters say the measure would combat tax evasion; opponents warn it could exclude people who rely on cash

Congress also approved the so-called “anti-meme law,” penalizing misuse of official government logos. Supporters say it targets fraud; opponents warn ambiguous wording could threaten satire and political criticism.

Culture

In San Cristóbal de las Casas, a new textile conservation laboratory will repair damaged garments and protect the Maya World Textile Center’s 3,400-piece collection from insects and fungi. Other traditions found an audience onstage: 12 delegations brought music and masked dances to Oaxaca’s first Afro Guelaguetza, a dedicated celebration of Afro-Mexican heritage in Chacahua Isla. Further afield, Ballet Folklórico will celebrate its 75th anniversary with a 24-city U.S. tour, featuring regional dances and live music.

Other news from across Mexico

Looking ahead

The week ends with tariff relief still unresolved and new payments legislation awaiting promulgation. The Federal Reserve’s Oct. 27–28 meeting, followed by Banxico’s Nov. 5 decision, will put interest rates back in focus after the peso’s recent slide. Businesses and consumers will also be watching for Hacienda’s designation of sectors facing cash-payment restrictions once the legislation takes effect. Meanwhile, across Mexico, families and communities are preparing to remember their dead on Nov. 1–2.

Mexico News Daily

World.content:

Angham at the new opera house, three nights of jazz and the film festival from 11 November. The month, day by day.

Evening crowds on Al-Sherifein Street in downtown Cairo. (File photo)

CAIRO — This guide is for expats, digital nomads and long-stay visitors who want to plan a full month of things to do in Cairo November 2026, not just a weekend of sightseeing.November is one of the best months to be out in Cairo.

The heat has usually broken and evenings are cooler, with jazz, film, theatre and comedy across the city.The first week brings Angham at the New Capital Opera House and the Cairo International Jazz Festival.

The middle of the month brings the Cairo International Film Festival, Max Amini in English and Heba Tawaji at Fustat, a historic park and arena in Old Cairo.Prices below come from the event pages on Ticketsmarche, a Cairo ticketing platform.

Prices converted at about EGP 55.8 per US$ (RT, a financial-data provider, 25 October 2026). The New Administrative Capital, the government’s new city east of Cairo, is far from the centre, so ride-hailing is the practical option.

4 to 7 November: Opera, Jazz and Theatre

Wednesday 4 November and Friday 6 November Angham at the New Capital Opera House Main Hall, City of Arts and Culture, New Administrative Capital · EGP 6,500 to EGP 250,000 (about US$117 to US$4,480) across seven categories · Show time not published Egyptian singer Angham is billed as the first Egyptian and Arab woman to perform in the opera house’s Main Hall, on Egyptian Love Day. A second show on 6 November was added after the first night sold out.

Wednesday 4 to Friday 6 November, 4:30 pm and 8:00 pm Redeeming Love Falaki Mainstage Theater, Abdeen, Cairo · EGP 300 (about US$5) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Thursday 5 to Saturday 7 November Cairo International Jazz Festival 2026 American University in Cairo (AUC) Tahrir Square campus, Downtown · Price not published here The festival’s 18th edition lists more than 15 concerts over three days, with artists from eight countries including Egypt, Denmark and Portugal. It also runs workshops, jazz talks and jam sessions.

Thursday 5 November Gala de Danza Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM), Giza · Time and price not published A one-evening gala of ballet and contemporary dance is staged inside the Grand Egyptian Museum, Egypt’s new museum beside the Giza pyramids. Book through the museum’s official channels.

Thursday 5 November, 9:00 pm Nour Hajjar Stand-Up Show Teatro 90, a theatre in New Cairo · EGP 1,000 to EGP 1,500 (about US$18 to US$27) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Friday 6 November, 8:00 pm Ali Quandil: Ameed El Shabab El Single Teatro 90, New Cairo · EGP 800 to EGP 1,200 (about US$14 to US$22) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Friday 6 November, 8:30 pm Shawshy Time El Rihany Theater, Downtown Cairo · EGP 300 to EGP 400 (about US$5 to US$7) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Saturday 7 November, 8:00 pm Koala Sandwich Live Teatro 90, New Cairo · EGP 500 to EGP 700 (about US$9 to US$13) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

11 to 14 November: Film, Fustat and Comedy in English

Wednesday 11 to Friday 20 November Cairo International Film Festival Cairo Opera House, Gezira, Egypt’s main opera venue · Ticket details on the festival website Egypt’s long-running international film festival runs for ten days from 11 November, with its headquarters at the Cairo Opera House. Check the official programme for venues and ticket details.

Thursday 12 to Saturday 14 and Wednesday 18 November, several shows a day Max Amini Live in Cairo St. Regis hotel, New Administrative Capital · Prices on Ticketsmarche · Tickets on Ticketsmarche An international stand-up comedian performs in English, with early and late shows. Several dates are listed as sold out, so check availability first.

Thursday 12 November, 8:00 pm Meen Amin Ewart Memorial Hall, AUC Tahrir Square · EGP 750 to EGP 2,000 (about US$13 to US$36) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Friday 13 November, 9:45 pm Heba Tawaji at Fustat Festival Fustat, Old Cairo · EGP 900 to EGP 3,000 (about US$16 to US$54) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche A concert by the Lebanese singer Heba Tawaji at Fustat. Arrive early to explore Old Cairo before the show.

Saturday 14 November, 8:00 pm El Leila El Kebira x Theatro Arkan Theatro Arkan, a theatre in Arkan Plaza, Sheikh Zayed · EGP 550 to EGP 1,050 (about US$10 to US$19) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche A puppet show listed on Ticketsmarche for this date.

20 to 28 November: Oud, Fustat and Stand-Up

Friday 20 November, 8:30 pm Saad El Oud Ewart Memorial Hall, AUC Tahrir Square · EGP 700 to EGP 1,200 (about US$13 to US$22) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Friday 27 November, 9:30 pm Tamer Ashour Fustat, Old Cairo · EGP 800 to EGP 8,334 (about US$14 to US$149) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Saturday 28 November, 8:00 pm Sammy Obeid: The Wit Supremacy Tour Teatro 90, New Cairo · EGP 1,000 to EGP 2,000 (about US$18 to US$36) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Saturday 28 November, 8:00 pm Al Gomhour Yoghani Theatro Arkan, Sheikh Zayed · EGP 500 to EGP 1,500 (about US$9 to US$27) · Tickets on Ticketsmarche

Planning Your Cairo in November

November in Cairo is usually mild by day and cool at night, with little rain. Carry a light jacket for evening events.

No nationwide Egyptian public holiday is confirmed for November 2026. Religious holidays follow the Islamic calendar and can be announced late, so check government notices if you need public services.

Getting around at night is easiest by ride-hailing app, especially for venues in New Cairo, Sheikh Zayed and the New Administrative Capital. Plan your return in advance.

Egypt’s weekend is Friday and Saturday, so many evening events fall on those nights. Several Max Amini shows are sold out, so book early.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the biggest events in Cairo in November 2026?

Angham performs at the New Capital Opera House on 4 and 6 November. The Cairo International Jazz Festival runs 5 to 7 November, and the Cairo International Film Festival opens on 11 November.

When is the Cairo International Film Festival 2026?

It runs from 11 to 20 November, with its headquarters at the Cairo Opera House.

Is November a good month to visit Cairo?

Yes. November usually has mild daytime temperatures, cool evenings and little rain, which suits outdoor and evening events.

Where can I buy tickets for Cairo events in November 2026?

Most concerts, plays and comedy shows listed here sell through Ticketsmarche, a Cairo ticketing platform. The film and jazz festivals publish ticket details on their own websites.

Are there any public holidays in Egypt in November 2026?

No nationwide public holiday is confirmed for November 2026. Religious holidays can be announced late, so check official government notices.

World.title: What to Do in Durban in November 2026: Triathlon, Theatre and French Wine
World.content:
DURBAN · Culture

TinMan Durban takes over the beachfront on 8 November, and a French wine evening follows in Umhlanga on 26 November. Thirteen confirmed events, day by day.

DURBAN — This is the monthly culture and events guide for expats, digital nomads and long-stay visitors, with things to do in Durban November 2026 listed in date order. Every card was checked against the organiser or Webtickets, a South African online ticket seller.

Wednesday 4 November is a one-off public holiday for the local government elections, so expect shops, banks and transport to run on holiday hours. Rand prices are converted at about R16.6 per US$ (RT, a financial-data provider, 25 October 2026).

1 to 8 November: Theatre, Music and the Beachfront Race

Sunday 1 November, 14:00 How to Cook Your Husband Rhumbelow Theatre, Cunningham Road, Umbilo · R180 (about US$11) The Rhumbelow is a community-run cabaret theatre in Umbilo, and this Sunday matinee is part of a run that began on 31 October. You can bring a picnic basket or buy food at the venue, and doors open 90 minutes before the show.

Saturday 7 November, 10:00 Durban Doek & Slay Motown Club, Durban · R150–R250 (about US$9–US$15) This is a ladies-only daytime celebration with live artists and DJs. The organisers ask guests to follow a denim and white dress code, so plan your outfit ahead.

Saturday 7 November, 19:00 Nathi Mankayi: The Buyelekhaya Tour Opera Theatre, The Playhouse Company, Anton Lembede Street, Durban Central · Price not published The Playhouse Company is Durban’s main performing arts complex. Mankayi, an Afro-soul singer, plays a stripped-back concert with a live band, and tickets are sold through Webtickets.

Saturday 7 November, 19:30, and Sunday 8 November, 14:00 You Asked for It – 4! The Reals Rhumbelow Theatre, Cunningham Road, Umbilo · R180–R220 (about US$11–US$13) The organiser says booking is essential for this two-show weekend. Choose the Sunday afternoon show if you prefer to be home before dark.

Sunday 8 November, from 07:00 TinMan Durban Suncoast Casino, Hotels and Entertainment, Durban beachfront · from R180 (about US$11) TinMan is a South African multisport series, and this round includes a 10 km run and several triathlon distances. Race-day registration is at the Suncoast Sundeck from 05:45 to 07:00, so arrive early.

14 and 15 November: Outdoors, Music and a Half Marathon

Saturday 14 November, 09:00 to 18:00, and Sunday 15 November, 09:00 to 16:00 Great Outdoors Expo 2026 Durban Exhibition Centre, 11 Walnut Road, Durban Central · R40–R100 (about US$2.40–US$6) An outdoor, camping and 4×4 trade show with gear to inspect in person. Go on Saturday if you want the longer opening hours.

Saturday 14 November, 16:00 The R&B Movement: 4th Anniversary Outdoor Experience Cappello Umhlanga, Umhlanga · R250 (about US$15) Umhlanga is a seaside suburb north of Durban. The event was postponed from an earlier date to 14 November, and the organisers promise DJs playing R&B from the early 1990s to today.

Saturday 14 November, 16:00 Henry Ate at DoughPamine DoughPamine, Slow Roads Collective, Salt Rock · R350 (about US$21) Salt Rock is a coastal town on the North Coast. The organisers invite guests to bring picnic gear, cooler boxes, and their own food and drinks for a backyard evening.

Sunday 15 November, early morning start Umhlanga Rocks Half-Marathon 2026 Oceans Mall, Umhlanga · Entry fee not published The race offers 21.1 km, 10 km and 5 km distances. Check the running calendar listing and the organiser before you travel, because entries and fees were still to be confirmed.

25 to 29 November: Comedy, French Wine and Saturday Shows

Wednesday 25 to Saturday 28 November, 19:30, and Sunday 29 November, 14:00 Schlep with Beryl Cohen: Lilly Slaptsilli Rhumbelow Theatre, Cunningham Road, Umbilo · R280 (about US$17) This run of five shows is sold with allocated seating at tables of eight. Alcohol may not be brought in, but a bar and food are available.

Thursday 26 November, 17:30 Beaujolais Nouveau 2026: A French Celebration in Durban Beverly Hills Hotel, Umhlanga · R650 (about US$39) Beaujolais Nouveau is a young French red wine released each November. The ticket covers the wine while stocks last, canapés, a buffet dinner, live music and a DJ, and a charity raffle is planned.

Saturday 28 November, 17:00 The Somnyama Show: Durban Third Edition The Villa, Mahatma Gandhi Road, Point, Durban · R150–R250 (about US$9–US$15) This is an early-evening show in the Point area of Durban. Book ahead on Webtickets, then allow time for evening traffic.

Saturday 28 November, 20:00 Two and a Half Charous playTSOGO Globe, Suncoast, Durban beachfront · R100–R300 (about US$6–US$18) Pair this with the earlier Somnyama Show if you want a full Saturday out. The Globe is inside the Suncoast complex, where the beachfront parking fills quickly on show nights.

Planning Your Durban in November

South Africa has no regular national public holiday in November, but the President declared Wednesday 4 November 2026 a public holiday for the local government elections. Check opening hours for that day before you plan an errand or a trip.

Webtickets sells most of the events above, and the Rhumbelow Theatre also lists its shows on its own events page. Prices shown are the lowest and highest published on the day of checking and can change as shows sell out.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “US draft ends UN force in Western Sahara in 2027” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Getting around at night is easiest by ride-hailing app or pre-booked taxi, especially between the beachfront, Umbilo and Umhlanga. On Sunday 8 November parts of the beachfront near the TinMan course may be busy, so leave extra time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the biggest event in Durban in November 2026?

TinMan Durban on Sunday 8 November is the largest single event, a multisport race at the Suncoast beachfront starting at 07:00. Entry starts at R180 (about US$11).

Where can I buy tickets for Durban events in November 2026?

Webtickets, a South African online ticket seller, lists most events in this guide, including the Rhumbelow Theatre shows, TinMan Durban and the Great Outdoors Expo. Some events may also sell at the venue.

Is there a public holiday in Durban in November 2026?

Yes, one. President Ramaphosa declared Wednesday 4 November 2026 a public holiday for the local government elections. South Africa has no regular national public holiday in November.

What can I do in Durban on Saturday 14 November 2026?

The Great Outdoors Expo runs from 09:00 to 18:00 at the Durban Exhibition Centre. At 16:00 there are two music events: the R&B Movement anniversary in Umhlanga and Henry Ate in Salt Rock.

DAR ES SALAAM · Culture

Ten confirmed events fill Dar es Salaam in November 2026, from a security summit on 7 November to a property expo from 20 to 22 November. Here is the month, day by day.

The Dar es Salaam waterfront seen from the harbour. (File photo)

DAR ES SALAAM — This monthly guide is for people who live here, not weekend tourists. It lists the things to do in Dar es Salaam in November 2026 that we could confirm with the organiser, venue or ticket seller.

The month starts with a security summit at the Julius Nyerere International Convention Centre, the city’s main conference hall. Live shows and a boxing night follow at The Super Dome, an entertainment venue in Masaki, an upmarket coastal neighbourhood.

Mid-month, three trade fairs open at the Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, an exhibition hall in Upanga. Prices in Tanzanian shillings (TZS) are converted at about TZS 2,630 per US$ (RT, a financial-data provider, 23 October 2026).

5 to 7 November: Summit and Music

Friday 6 November, evening Music Festival The Super Dome, Masaki · Price not published The venue calendar lists this festival for the evening of 6 November but names no acts. Check the venue page for ticket news before you plan the evening.

Saturday 7 November, 6:00 PM International Peace and Security Summit 2026, 2nd Edition Julius Nyerere International Convention Centre, Shaaban Robert Street, city centre · Regular TZS 100,000 (about US$38), VIP TZS 150,000 (about US$57), VVIP TZS 300,000 (about US$114) Tickets are sold through Ticketsasa, a Tanzanian online ticket seller, in three tiers. The listing names no speakers, so read the programme before you pay for a higher tier.

Saturday 7 November, evening Mbili Abel Concert The Super Dome, Masaki · Price not published The venue calendar lists this concert for the evening of 7 November, the same night as the summit across town. Choose one early, because traffic between the two venues can be slow.

9 to 14 November: Business Summit, Boxing and Gospel Awards

Monday 9 to Wednesday 11 November Africa Connect (AFRICON) Leadership, Investment & Entrepreneurship Summit and Awards 2026 Julius Nyerere International Convention Centre, city centre · Free registration listed The organiser, Leading Women of Africa, takes sign-ups on Luma, an online event registration platform. The programme includes business-to-government meetings on 10 November, so register early if you want a meeting slot.

Friday 13 November, evening Boxing Event The Super Dome, Masaki · Price not published The venue calendar lists a boxing night on 13 November without naming the fighters. Ask the venue for ticket details closer to the date.

Saturday 14 November, evening East Africa Gospel Music Awards (EAGMA) 2026 The Super Dome, Masaki · Price not published The venue says the awards honour gospel music from seven East African countries. Expect a long evening, so plan your transport home in advance.

18 to 22 November: Trade Fairs and Property

Wednesday 18 to Friday 20 November, 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM 27th Autoexpo Tanzania 2026 Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, Malik Road, Upanga · Free admission listed Expo Group, a Dubai trade-fair organiser, stages this motor-trade show for cars, spare parts and accessories. Go on the first day for the widest choice of exhibitors.

Wednesday 18 to Friday 20 November, 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM 26th Indusmach Tanzania 2026 Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, Malik Road, Upanga · Price not published This Expo Group show covers industrial machinery and manufacturing equipment. It runs on the same days and at the same venue as the car and hardware shows, so one trip covers all three.

Wednesday 18 to Friday 20 November, 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM 7th Tools & Hardware Tanzania 2026 Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, Malik Road, Upanga · Price not published Expo Group lists tools, hardware, materials and machinery for this edition. It is useful if you are renovating or buying building supplies, so bring a list of what you need.

Friday 20 to Sunday 22 November Tanzania Real Estate Expo (TAREX) 2026 The Super Dome, Masaki · Price not published TAREX is a three-day property exhibition at the Super Dome, an entertainment venue in Masaki. Foreign residents weighing a home purchase should check ownership rules for non-citizens before visiting any developer stand.

Planning Your Dar es Salaam November

No Tanzania-wide public holiday is listed for November 2026, and the next fixed national holiday is Independence Day on 9 December. Offices, banks and shops should keep normal hours, but confirm any one-off announcement with the government.

Getting around at night is easiest by taxi or ride-hailing app, especially for events in Masaki and the city centre. Leave early before evening events, because traffic can build up around both areas.

For updates, check the calendars of The Super Dome and the Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre, and the organiser pages listed below. Venue calendars list dates but often not prices, so confirm tickets before you travel.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the biggest events in Dar es Salaam in November 2026?

The Africa Connect summit runs from 9 to 11 November, three trade fairs run from 18 to 20 November, and the Tanzania Real Estate Expo runs from 20 to 22 November.

Where are the November trade fairs held?

Autoexpo, Indusmach and Tools & Hardware Tanzania run from 18 to 20 November at the Diamond Jubilee Expo Centre in Upanga, from 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM, according to the organiser, Expo Group.

How much is the International Peace and Security Summit?

Tickets cost TZS 100,000 (about US$38) for Regular, TZS 150,000 (about US$57) for VIP and TZS 300,000 (about US$114) for VVIP. The summit starts at 6:00 PM on Saturday 7 November.

Is there a public holiday in Dar es Salaam in November 2026?

We found no Tanzania-wide public holiday listed for November 2026. The next fixed national holiday is Independence Day on 9 December, so offices and banks should keep normal hours.

The San Miguel International Jazz & Blues Festival runs from 11 to 15 November 2026 in the city centre.

SAN MIGUEL DE ALLENDE — This guide is for people who live here or are staying for weeks, not for a quick weekend. It covers the things to do in San Miguel de Allende in November 2026 that organisers have confirmed, with dates, venues and prices.

November opens with the last Day of the Dead events on Sunday 1 November, then moves to a youth reading fair and the jazz festival. All prices were converted at about MXN 18.65 per US$.

Several 1 November events have no published ticket price yet, so check with the venue before you go.

1 to 6 November: Day of the Dead Finale and a Reading Fair

Sunday 1 November, 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Sunday brunch with a guest traditional cook Hacienda El Santuario, Aldama 41, Centro · Price not published Part of the Muerte en Vida IV Festival, a Day of the Dead programme. Tickets were not on sale at the time of writing, so ask the venue about booking.

Sunday 1 November, 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. Exhibición de ofrendas (altar exhibition) Jardín Allende, Principal 18, Centro · Price not published A midday slot is the calmest way to see traditional Day of the Dead altars. Go before the evening events draw the crowds.

Sunday 1 November, 6:00 p.m. Requiem by Michael Haydn Templo de San Francisco (a church), San Francisco and Juárez, Centro · Price not published The San Miguel de Allende Philharmonic Choir and Orchestra perform this requiem, a classical mass for the dead, in a historic church. Tickets were not on sale at the time of writing, so check the venue first.

Sunday 1 November, 6:00 p.m. Huesos, calacas y calaveras: puppet theatre Jardín Allende, Principal 18, Centro · Price not published A puppet show with the characters El Catrín and La Catrina, the elegant skeleton couple of Day of the Dead tradition. Spanish helps, but the staging is visual.

Sunday 1 November, 6:00 p.m. Antojitos de Coyoacán Hacienda El Santuario, Aldama 41, Centro · Price not published Live music and Mexican street-food flavours as part of the Muerte en Vida IV Festival. Plan to eat there, and ask about entry costs in advance.

Wednesday 4 to Friday 6 November Feria de la Lectura: “Entre castillos y dragones” Centro para los Adolescentes de San Miguel de Allende (CASA), a youth centre and library · Price not published A three-day reading fair with storytelling, workshops and games on fantasy literature. It suits families and anyone who wants to practise Spanish in a relaxed setting.

11 to 15 November: San Miguel Jazz and Blues Festival

Wednesday 11 November, 1:00 p.m. Educational concert: Antonio Lozoya Jazz Trio Casa Nigromante (University of Guanajuato, UG), Umarán 38, Centro · Free A daytime concert that sets the scene for the festival. It is a low-cost way to hear the music before the ticketed evening shows.

Thursday 12 November, 1:00 p.m. Film screening: The Story of Benny Goodman Casa Nigromante (University of Guanajuato, UG), Umarán 38, Centro · Free A free afternoon film from the festival programme. Arrive a little early, as seating at university venues can be limited.

Thursday 12 November, 6:00 p.m. Gypsy Jazz: Hot Club de San Miguel Teatro Ángela Peralta, Mesones 82, Centro, the city’s main historic theatre · MXN 440 (about US$24) A local gypsy-jazz group opens the festival’s evening programme in the city centre. Buy tickets on the festival website, which is the organiser.

Friday 13 November, 1:00 p.m. Film screening: Born to Be Blue (the Chet Baker story) Casa Nigromante (University of Guanajuato, UG), Umarán 38, Centro · Free A second free film in the festival’s daytime programme. Pair it with a late lunch in the centre before the evening concert.

Friday 13 November, 6:00 p.m. Eric “Slim” Miller Blues Band (United States) Teatro Ángela Peralta, Mesones 82, Centro · MXN 660 (about US$35) A US blues band, and a change of pace from the acoustic jazz sets. Tickets are sold through the festival website.

Saturday 14 November, 6:00 p.m. Mar Vilaseca Jazz Quartet (Spain and United States) Teatro Ángela Peralta, Mesones 82, Centro · Platea (stalls) MXN 770 (about US$41); luneta, palco and galería (upper levels) MXN 660 (about US$35) Seating is priced in two tiers, so choose by budget. Book ahead if you want the stalls.

Sunday 15 November, 6:00 p.m. Tribute to Sting with Becks Bustamante (Mexico and United States) Centro Cultural, Instituto Allende (a cultural centre), Ancha de San Antonio 22, Centro · MXN 770 (about US$41) The closing concert of the festival moves to the Instituto Allende cultural centre. Tickets are on the festival website.

Planning Your November in San Miguel de Allende

Monday 16 November is a public holiday in Mexico, observed for Revolution Day under the Federal Labour Law. The anniversary itself falls on Friday 20 November, and we could not confirm a San Miguel programme for it.

For festival tickets, use the San Miguel Jazz Festival website, the organiser’s own ticket page. For the other events, ask the venue directly, since several had no public prices when we checked.

Visit San Miguel, the city tourism board’s event list, is the best place to watch for time changes and late additions. All times in this guide are local time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the biggest event in San Miguel de Allende in November 2026?

The San Miguel International Jazz & Blues Festival runs from 11 to 15 November. Evening concerts are at Teatro Ángela Peralta on 12 to 14 November and at Instituto Allende on 15 November.

How much are the jazz festival tickets?

Evening concerts cost MXN 440 to MXN 770 (about US$24 to US$41), depending on the show and seat. Prices converted at about MXN 18.65 per US$. Tickets are sold on the festival website.

Are there free events during the jazz festival?

Yes. An educational concert on 11 November and film screenings on 12 and 13 November are free. All start at 1:00 p.m. at Casa Nigromante, Umarán 38.

Is 16 November 2026 a public holiday in Mexico?

Yes. Mexico observes Revolution Day on the third Monday of November, which is 16 November 2026, under the Federal Labour Law. The anniversary itself is Friday 20 November.

What is happening on 1 November in San Miguel de Allende?

Day of the Dead events continue: an altar exhibition at Jardín Allende from 12:00 p.m., plus a Michael Haydn requiem and a puppet show at 6:00 p.m., in the Templo de San Francisco and Jardín Allende.

World.title: Lin-Manuel Miranda Surprises San Juan Crowd
World.content:
Entertainment: Puerto Rico

Key Facts Who. Lin-Manuel Miranda, the creator of the Broadway musical Hamilton, appeared unannounced at the show’s second performance on 24 October.

Where. Buena Vista Social Club, a Broadway musical, plays in Spanish at the Antonio Paoli Festival Hall in San Juan.

Why it matters. The Broadway co-producers call it the first Puerto Rico staging licensed independently while the original still runs.

As of 25 October 2026, 22:30 GMT

Miranda made a surprise appearance at a San Juan theatre on Saturday evening, 24 October. The audience gave him a standing ovation during the Spanish-language Puerto Rican production of Buena Vista Social Club.

The Lin-Manuel Miranda surprise appearance came at the second performance of Buena Vista Social Club in Puerto Rico. The run opened on 23 October 2026 at a theatre in Santurce, a district of San Juan.

What Happened at the Performance

Miranda appeared unannounced at the Sala de Festivales Antonio Paoli, the Antonio Paoli Festival Hall, on Saturday evening, 24 October. The hall is part of the Centro de Bellas Artes de Santurce, or Santurce Performing Arts Center, in San Juan.

Ender Vega, the producer at BAS Entertainment, the company staging the show, recognised him publicly. Vega thanked Miranda for supporting the production’s arrival in Puerto Rico, and the audience gave him a standing ovation.

In Spanish, Miranda said “Gracias por apoyar el teatro”, meaning “Thank you for supporting theatre”. He added that bringing one of his favourite shows “con un elenco boricua, en español”, or with a Puerto Rican cast in Spanish, left him “sin palabras”, or speechless.

A street in Santurce, San Juan. (File photo)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Spanish-Language Show With a Puerto Rican Cast

The musical celebrates the legacy of the Buena Vista Social Club, the Havana music collective whose 1990s album and film made the Cuban music style son famous worldwide. This production is performed in Spanish, with an all-Puerto Rican cast and musicians.

Choco Orta plays Omara, Michael Stuart plays Ibrahim and Ernesto Concepción plays Compay. Modesto Lacén is Juan de Marcos, René Monclova is Rubén, and Luis Sanz plays Eliades on the cuatro, a ten-string Puerto Rican instrument similar to a guitar.

Why It Matters for US Readers

Puerto Rico is a US territory, and its residents are US citizens. Buena Vista Social Club is a Tony-winning Broadway musical, now staged in Spanish on US soil.

The Broadway original opened on 19 March 2025 and won four Tony Awards, Broadway’s top prizes, plus a Special Tony, an honorary award, for its band. It had 10 nominations, and its cast album won the 2026 Grammy, a leading US music award, for Best Musical Theater Album.

Miranda and his father, Luis A. Miranda Jr., are co-producers of the Broadway original. They issued a joint statement calling the Puerto Rico run an important milestone for the island’s professional theatre community and its relationship with Broadway.

According to the Broadway co-producers, it is the first production on the archipelago granted an independent performance licence while the Broadway show is still running. BAS Entertainment stages the Puerto Rican premiere by special agreement with the Broadway producing team.

What Is Not Known

It is not confirmed whether Miranda attended any other night of the run. It is also not known whether he will attend future performances.

Ticket availability beyond the listed dates is not confirmed. The upcoming performances listed so far are 31 October and 1 November 2026.

What It Means for Visitors and Fans

Upcoming performances are listed for Saturday 31 October and Sunday 1 November 2026 at the Antonio Paoli hall. The producer says tickets are sold through Ticketera.com, a ticketing website.

Availability is not confirmed, so visitors should check with the venue before planning a trip. Expect a Spanish-language show with a Puerto Rican cast.

For now, the Puerto Rican staging has drawn public support from a co-producer of the Broadway show. What happens after 1 November is not yet confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Lin-Manuel Miranda attend Buena Vista Social Club in Puerto Rico?

Yes. He made a surprise appearance at the second performance on Saturday evening, 24 October 2026, at the Antonio Paoli Festival Hall in San Juan.

Who is in the Puerto Rican cast?

Choco Orta, Michael Stuart, Ernesto Concepción, Modesto Lacén, René Monclova and Luis Sanz are among the cast. The cast and musicians are all Puerto Rican, and the show is performed in Spanish.

When are the next performances and how do I buy tickets?

Performances are listed for 31 October and 1 November 2026. The producer says tickets are available through Ticketera.com, and availability should be checked with the venue.

Is the Puerto Rico production approved by the Broadway team?

Yes. BAS Entertainment produces the Puerto Rican premiere by special agreement with the Broadway producing team.

World.title: Serbia Projection Shows Students Winning 52%
World.content:
Published Sunday, 25 October, 6:05 p.m. Eastern Time (ET) · Source: Ipsos, CeSID, Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), Kalshi

Key Facts Projection: Ipsos, a polling firm, and CeSID, a Serbian election monitor, give the student-backed list 52%.

Rival: Aleksandar Vučić’s United Serbia list, led by his Progressive Party, gets 39.3%, about 104 of 250 seats.

Status: A projection from a partial sample, not the official result.

Next: The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), Serbia’s election authority, must publish the full count within about four days.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US-regulated prediction market, prices the Student List at 98% to win, about 6:00 p.m. ET.

A student-backed list is heading for a clear majority in Serbia’s parliamentary election, according to the first projection from Ipsos and CeSID. It puts the Student List at 52% of the vote and Aleksandar Vučić’s list at 39.3%.

The projection is an estimate, not the official count. Our Serbia Election 2026 coverage follows every step, and we reported earlier that Vučić said his list had lost.

What the Projection Shows

Ipsos is an international polling company, and CeSID, the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy, is a Serbian group that monitors votes. Together they released the projection on Sunday evening, after polls closed at 20:00 Central European Time (CET), which is 3:00 p.m. ET.

They give the Student List, which campaigns as “Students Win”, 52% of the vote and about 138 of the 250 seats in the National Assembly. Vučić’s list, “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia”, gets 39.3% and about 104 seats.

Reports differ by one seat on the student total, 138 or 139, so we give the rounded figure. A party needs 126 seats for a majority, so on these numbers the Student List would not need a coalition partner.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How Reliable Is an Early Projection?

A projection is built from a sample of polling stations, weighted to stand in for the whole country. The Sunday evening projection came from a partial sample, so it is not final.

The picture can still move as more stations report. The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), the state body that runs the vote, counted only 203 of 8,392 polling stations when it published its first tally, which had Vučić’s list ahead. Early counts depend on which stations report first.

Why Turnout Matters

Turnout passed 67% an hour before polls closed, according to the interim figures. Many Serbians treated the vote as a verdict on Vučić’s rule.

The vote followed the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in the Serbian city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The disaster set off student-led protests that lasted almost two years and produced the Student List.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi, the Student List was priced at 98% to win the parliamentary election and the list led by Vučić’s long-ruling Serbian Progressive Party at 4% at about 6:00 p.m. ET on 25 October. The market had traded 142,530 contracts.

A separate Kalshi market prices a student vote share of at least 50% at 86%. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), and its prices are bets, not polls. The two prices come from separate contracts and can add up to more than 100%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

File photo: Republic Square in Belgrade.

What It Means for You

For a reader in the United States, a defeat for the leader who has dominated Serbia for over a decade would reshape the Western Balkans, a region of former Yugoslav states. It would also test Serbia’s ties with Russia and China against its long-stalled bid to join the European Union.

Investors in Serbian debt and companies should watch the final count and any coalition talks, because policy continuity is the open question.

What Is Not Known

The official RIK result and seat distribution are not yet known. We also cannot yet say which smaller lists cleared the 3% threshold, or how quickly a government could form.

World.title: Spain’s Campaign Heats Up as Polls Split
World.content:
Pedro Sánchez speaks at La Moncloa in Madrid (file photo, 28 May 2024). Photo: Pool Moncloa/Borja Puig de la Bellacasa, via Wikimedia Commons.

Spain’s main parties stepped up campaigning over the weekend of 23 to 25 October 2026, five weeks before the general election on 29 November, as our Spain Election 2026 dossier tracks. Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo promised a smaller state in Valencia on Friday, while polls disagree sharply on who leads.

A private poll published on Friday puts the conservative People’s Party narrowly ahead. The state-run Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) still shows the governing Socialists well in front.

Key Facts Vote: Spain votes on Sunday, 29 November; the official campaign runs 13 to 27 November.

Polls: IMOP, a private pollster, has the People’s Party (PP) first at 28.5%; the state-run CIS has the Socialists (PSOE) on 34.0%.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the CFTC (the Commodity Futures Trading Commission), priced Feijóo at 82% to be prime minister (25 October, 5:52 p.m. ET).

Unknown: Spain’s Supreme Court has yet to rule on 163,000 disputed overseas voter registrations.

This story is part of our coverage of the Spain Election 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Spain's New Parliament Meets December 23

Campaign Events

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), told supporters in Valencia on Friday, 23 October, that a PP government would shrink the state. He also promised to exempt minimum-wage earners from the personal income tax, known as IRPF.

Pedro Sánchez, the Socialist (PSOE) prime minister, recorded a video message defending his anti-war position at Madrid’s Reina Sofía, the national art museum, on Saturday, 24 October. Santiago Abascal, leader of the conservative Vox party, told a rally in Palma the same day to stay on “maximum alert” on 29 November and spoke of possible electoral fraud; the reports we reviewed offered no evidence of any.

On Saturday in Barcelona, the left-wing Podemos party and the Catalan Republican Left (ERC) presented an electoral pact. Podemos is to stay off the Catalan ballot, while ERC’s Gabriel Rufián campaigns for the arrangement elsewhere in Spain; it is a pact, not a coalition.

The Congress of Deputies in Madrid, where the new parliament will convene. File photo.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Polling Divide

IMOP, a Spanish polling firm, published a survey on 23 October. It put the PP at 28.5%, the PSOE at 27.1% and Vox at 20.0%, and projected 123 seats for the PP, 113 for the PSOE and 72 for Vox in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies.

IMOP’s reading is the latest private poll we could verify, and we cannot confirm a polling average from the sources available, so we do not quote one.The CIS survey, taken on 1 to 6 October and published on 14 October, differs sharply.

It shows the PSOE at 34.0%, the PP at 22.2%, Vox at 17.1% and the left-wing Sumar-Frente Amplio alliance at 6.1%, from more than 5,000 interviews.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi’s market “Prime Minister of Spain after the next election?”, traders priced Alberto Núñez Feijóo at 82%, Pedro Sánchez at 18% and Santiago Abascal at 6% on 25 October at 5:52 p.m. ET. Kalshi is regulated in the US by the CFTC, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and about 23,951 contracts had traded.

Vox is a right-wing party and the PP’s likely partner. The prices come from separate contracts, so they need not add to 100%.

These prices are bets, not polls, and can move quickly as new information emerges.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Election Timetable

The vote covers both chambers of parliament, the Congress of Deputies and the Senate. The sources we checked give no polling-station hours and no new Senate projection.

Institutional Uncertainty

The main open legal question is the status of about 163,000 disputed overseas voter registrations. The Constitutional Court reportedly declined to admit an appeal from the Ombudsman, the state’s rights watchdog, as premature, which leaves the Supreme Court to decide whether the registrations can affect the November vote.

The politics rest on the gap between private polls and the CIS, which puts the Socialists nearly 12 points ahead of the PP (34.0% to 22.2%). The IMOP poll shows the opposite order, with the PP slightly ahead.

What It Means For US Readers

For US investors and policy watchers, the 29 November vote will decide whether a PP-led government, possibly leaning on Vox, a right-wing party, replaces Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition. That could shift Spain’s stance on European Union fiscal rules, energy policy and ties with Washington.

Markets and the latest private poll lean towards the right, but the CIS shows how far that picture could still change.

What Is Not Known

We also cannot say whether private polls or the CIS will prove more accurate on 29 November.No new verified Senate projection is available.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Spain’s general election?

Spain votes on Sunday, 29 November 2026, for both the Congress of Deputies and the Senate. The official campaign runs from 13 to 27 November.

Who is leading in the polls?

The latest private poll, IMOP on 23 October, puts the conservative PP narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE, with Vox third. The CIS survey shows the PSOE ahead by nearly 12 points.

What do prediction markets say?

On Kalshi, traders priced Feijóo at 82% to become prime minister on 25 October at 5:52 p.m. ET. These prices are bets, not polls.

World.title: Mexico City F1 Race Seen Adding US$1.2B
World.content:
Photo: ProtoplasmaKid / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

The capital’s chamber of commerce expects the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix to generate MXN 22.228 billion (about US$1.205 billion) in local economic activity, as the Mexico City F1 Grand Prix coverage follows the build-up to Sunday’s race. The estimate comes from Canaco CDMX, the Mexico City Chamber of Commerce, Services and Tourism.

The race is on Sunday, 1 November 2026, at 20:00 UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), which is 14:00 in Mexico City and 15:00 US Eastern Time. It is the weekend after the United States Grand Prix in Austin, Texas.

Key Facts Projection: Canaco CDMX, Mexico City’s chamber of commerce, expects MXN 22.228 billion (about US$1.205 billion) of activity from the race weekend.

Growth: Canaco puts that 6.5% above its 2025 projection of MXN 20.892 billion (about US$1.13 billion).

Race: Sunday, 1 November, 15:00 US Eastern Time, 71 laps at Mexico City’s Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez circuit.

Contract: Mexico’s race is guaranteed through 2028; talks on an extension are expected soon.

What The Chamber Counts

Canaco CDMX says ticket sales account for the largest share, about MXN 8.42 billion (about US$456 million). Tour guides, travel agencies and transfers add about MXN 4.518 billion (about US$245 million).

The chamber expects hotel occupancy of 85% to 95% around the circuit. It also expects gains for lodging, restaurants, transport and entertainment across the city.

We convert at about 18.45 pesos per US dollar, the rate implied by Canaco’s headline pair of figures. Last year’s edition drew 401,326 spectators over the weekend.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Why Sergio Pérez Matters

Sergio “Checo” Pérez, Mexico’s best-known Formula 1 driver, returns to the grid with Cadillac, the General Motors luxury brand and the new 11th team in the 2026 field. His teammate is Finland’s Valtteri Bottas.

Tickets for the race sold out well ahead of the weekend. Pérez’s home race is a large part of that appeal for Mexican fans.

Weekend Schedule

Practice 1, the first of three free-running sessions, runs on Friday, 30 October, from 18:30 to 19:30 UTC (14:30 to 15:30 US Eastern, 12:30 to 13:30 Mexico City). Practice 2 follows from 22:00 to 23:00 UTC.

On Saturday, 31 October, Practice 3 runs from 17:30 to 18:30 UTC and qualifying from 21:00 to 22:00 UTC. All times are from the official Formula 1 schedule.

Contract And Future

The current agreement guarantees the Mexican race through 2028. Organisers expect to start talks on a longer extension between late 2026 and early 2027.

Federico González Compeán, the race’s director general, has said the event wants an annual slot rather than sharing it with another venue. Organisers have rejected an alternating-year arrangement because the event needs year-round preparation.

Formula 2, the main support series, is expected to join the Mexico weekend from 2027.

What It Means For US Readers

For fans in the United States, the race falls on the day US clocks go back, so the 15:00 start is on Eastern Standard Time. The event is also a gauge of how much a single sporting weekend can add to a major Latin American city’s economy.

Cadillac’s presence gives American viewers a home-brand storyline.

What Is Not Known

The MXN 22.228 billion figure is a chamber projection, not audited post-event data. No contract beyond 2028 has been announced, and renewal talks have not concluded.

We found no active prediction market on the race result at the time of writing.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the 2026 Mexico City Grand Prix?

The race is on Sunday, 1 November 2026, at 20:00 UTC. That is 14:00 in Mexico City and 15:00 US Eastern Time.

How much activity does Canaco CDMX expect?

The chamber projects MXN 22.228 billion, about US$1.205 billion. It says that is 6.5% above the 2025 figure.

Who drives for Mexico?

Sergio “Checo” Pérez drives for Cadillac, alongside Valtteri Bottas. Cadillac is a new American team on the 2026 grid, backed by General Motors.

Is the race guaranteed beyond 2028?

No. The contract runs through 2028, and talks on an extension are expected between late 2026 and early 2027.
