World.title: Elecciones en Brasil 2026: las claves de una reñida segunda vuelta presidencial
World.content:
Casi 159 millones de brasileños están llamados a las urnas este domingo para decidir a su próximo presidente en lo que podría ser la elección más ajustada en la historia del país más poblado de América Latina. En la primera vuelta, el 4 de octubre, el hijo del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro se impuso con un 47% de los votos válidos (56,1 millones) por un 45% de Lula (53,9 millones), quien calificó el resultado como inesperado. Desde entonces, ambos candidatos han emprendido una intensa campaña tanto en redes sociales como en mitines multitudinarios en las calles con la mira puesta en el domingo 25 de octubre.

Más información Resultados de las elecciones en Brasil, en vivo

Mientras el triunfo de Lula supondría la continuidad y mantendría a Brasil junto con México como el último reducto de la izquierda en el renovado tablero político de Latinoamérica, una victoria de Bolsonaro marcaría el regreso del clan al poder y la consolidación definitiva de la ola ultra en el continente.

Más información Compare las propuestas de los candidatos para las elecciones de Brasil 2026

Una carrera presidencial en extremo igualada

Tres semanas después de la primera vuelta, la intensa movilización de la izquierda para consumar la remontada ha acortado la distancia entre ambos candidatos al mínimo. Según la encuesta más reciente de Datafolha, publicada la noche del jueves, la carrera presidencial se mantiene empatada con el 50% de preferencia de votos válidos para cada uno.

Se trata tanto de un empate numérico como de uno técnico, en el que la diferencia entre la preferencia efectiva de ambos es menor al margen de error (estimado en dos puntos) y, por lo tanto, resulta imposible inferir estadísticamente al candidato puntero. La más reciente encuesta de Quaest, encargada por Globo y divulgada el miércoles, apunta a tres sectores clave donde el porcentaje de indecisos ha aumentado ligeramente: las mujeres, los electores independientes y los beneficiarios que reciben la ayuda social Bolsa Familia.

El efecto de los debates

Uno de los factores que podría decantar la cerrada elección presidencial hacia un lado u otro está en el par de debates televisados, que los candidatos rechazaron antes de la primera vuelta. Después de protagonizar un primer cara a cara ríspido el domingo pasado, donde primaron las acusaciones de corrupción sobre las propuestas, el segundo debate, este viernes, se presenta como la última oportunidad de Lula y Bolsonaro para hablar al electorado a menos de 48 horas de la apertura de los colegios electorales. Y para atraerse los votos necesarios para sentenciar la disputa.

La jornada electoral y los resultados de la segunda vuelta

Para la segunda vuelta presidencial, los colegios electorales abrirán a las 08.00 de la mañana (hora de Brasilia) y cerrarán a las 17.00, nueve horas más tarde. A pesar de lo reñido de la contienda, el sistema de urnas electrónicas del Tribunal Superior Electoral, adoptado desde 1996, ofrece un escrutinio veloz al término de la jornada electoral sin pasar por conteos rápidos o sistemas de resultados preliminares.

En el papel, el voto en Brasil es obligatorio para los ciudadanos de 18 a 69 años, optativo para las personas de 16 y 17 años, los mayores de 70 y para quienes no saben leer ni escribir, la multa por ausentarse sin justificación ronda los tres reales (60 centavos de dólar); durante la primera vuelta del 4 de octubre el abstencionismo alcanzó un 20% del electorado, unos 33 millones de brasileños que si ahora comparecen podrían decidir la elección presidencial.

Con información de Naiara Galarraga Gortázar.

World.title: María Corina Machado regresa a Venezuela
World.content:
Después de casi 10 meses fuera del país, María Corina Machado, líder de la oposición antichavista y Premio Nobel de la Paz, ha regresado a Venezuela. “Estoy aquí, con ustedes”, ha escrito en sus redes sociales la dirigente opositora en la mañana del domingo. Poco después de su enigmático mensaje, el excandidato presidencial Edmundo González terminó por confirmar el regreso: “¡Venezuela! Me emociona muchísimo anunciarles que nuestra líder, mi querida María Corina, está en territorio venezolano. Hoy es un día importante para los venezolanos. ¡Nuestra voz soberana retorna con ella para liderar y encaminar este proceso!“, señaló, al tiempo que aseguró que “muy pronto” él también regresará.

La primera imagen de la opositora en su país ha sido en la Iglesia de Santa Rosa, en Barquisimeto, en el occidente de Venezuela. Los videos la muestran con varios rosarios al cuello, abrazando gente y con decenas de personas a las puertas del templo esperándola. Los videos registran un corto recorrido en una camioneta en el que decenas de personas la graban con sus celulares. “¡Vamos María tú puedes, estamos contigo!”, le gritaban. “Te esperábamos”, le gritaba otra señora. “¡Libertad!¡Libertad!“, jalearon en coro.

Más información El regreso de María Corina Machado a Venezuela, en vivo

La entrada de Machado, la dirigente con más respaldo según todas las encuestas, no ha sido sencilla. En los últimos tres meses, hubo al menos siete intentos en barcos, vuelos comerciales y privados y por tierra. Desde Virginia, en Estados Unidos, Panamá y Curazao. Todos fueron bloqueados, cancelados a última hora por averías o sin explicación. Aunque nadie de su entorno ha dicho públicamente quién le ha impedido viajar, no hay muchas dudas de que su salvoconducto dependía de la aprobación de Estados Unidos, con la que no contaba. La cadena Newsmax, próxima al trumpismo, aseguró que Machado entró por Colombia.

Su retorno lleva meses desencadenando un hervidero de rumores y versiones sin confirmar sobre su ingreso, y mantenía en alerta al gobierno chavista. La dirigente venezolana vuelve con la intención manifiesta de entrar de lleno en el juego político.

Su sola presencia en el país representa un desafío para Washington, que lleva meses intentando aplazar su regreso e incluso impidiéndolo, según han ido reportando varios medios en los últimos meses. Al ser preguntado por su regreso, Donald Trump ha dicho a los periodistas: “Espero que esté a salvo, es una mujer muy agradable”. Poco después, el secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, aseguró, sin celebrar explícitamente el la vuelta de Machado a Venezuela, que había sido posible como “resultado de las conversaciones apoyadas por Estados Unidos”.

También es un reto para los líderes del chavismo, que la consideran el enemigo público número uno. Aunque ahora el chavismo mantiene que no había vetado su vuelta y que incluso les puede suponer una ventaja política, al asumir que Machado se quemará rápidamente, pesan las advertencias de que deberá rendir cuentas a su regreso. El régimen la acusa, entre otras cosas, de haber promovido la invasión de Estados Unidos al país. El ministro del Interior, Diosdado Cabello, llegó a advertir en su programa de televisión: “No te diré cuál es la sorpresa que le tengo”.

El chavismo había dedicado mucha energía en los últimos meses a minar el liderazgo de la opositora y había logrado cierto respaldo de Washington, que dio señales de que, de momento, no quería a Machado en Venezuela. Pero volver a su país era clave para el futuro político de Machado. Aunque cuenta con la imagen positiva más alta entre los líderes políticos del país (un 57,4% de intención de voto, según la última encuesta de agosto Latam Pulse de AtlasIntel para Bloomberg), su incidencia en las decisiones políticas que se toman en el país que aspira a gobernar era nula.

Machado regresa con la intención de ponerse al frente de la oposición al chavismo ante un eventual, pero incierto, escenario electoral.

Pedro Urruchurtu Noselli, coordinador de Relaciones Internacionales de la dirigente opositora, celebró la llegada de María Corina Machado a Venezuela y expresó un explícito agradecimiento al Gobierno de Donald Trump. “Queremos expresar nuestro especial agradecimiento al presidente Trump, al secretario de Estado Marco Rubio y al Gobierno de los Estados Unidos por su compromiso y liderazgo”, dijo en una declaración pública difundida en X, en la que subrayó que las acciones del pasado 3 de enero, cuando Estados Unidos atacó Venezuela y detuvo al expresidente Nicolás Maduro, “abrieron un camino que hoy hace posible avanzar hacia una transición democrática”.

Urruchurtu dijo que el retorno de Machado tiene como fin acompañar a los venezolanos y “contribuir activamente a que este proceso avance de manera estable, pacífica y segura”, sentando las bases para la celebración de “elecciones presidenciales libres, justas y verificables”. El asesor político dijo que “este regreso fortalece las posibilidades de consolidar el cambio político, avanzar hacia la plena recuperación de las instituciones democráticas y permitir que los venezolanos puedan finalmente elegir libremente su futuro”.

Desde que se marchó de Venezuela en diciembre para recoger su Nobel de la Paz, Machado manejaba desde Washington —y después desde Panamá— su estrategia de lobismo para lograr volver al país. Mantenía diariamente reuniones con actores influyentes de todo el arco político para lograr un objetivo que no terminaba de concretarse y que empezaba a dibujarse sin ella. El entorno de Trump —auspiciado por el chavismo— llevaba meses apartándola hasta el punto de abrir una vía hacia la transición de Venezuela sin ella. “No puedo liderar este proceso desde el extranjero”, dijo a mediados de septiembre, días antes de intentar volver desde Panamá.

Desde el 1 de agosto, el Gobierno de Delcy Rodríguez y Dinorah Figuera —presidenta de la Asamblea Nacional de 2015, cuyo regreso al país fue respaldado por Estados Unidos— negociaron una hoja de ruta centrada en la renovación total del Tribunal Supremo de Justicia y del Consejo Nacional Electoral, banderas que también reivindicaba Machado. Pero la mesa contempla, además, la celebración de elecciones de gobernadores y alcaldes antes de las presidenciales, una fórmula que Machado había rechazado de plano y de forma explícita el pasado mes de mayo en una reunión con varios miembros de la oposición.

No fue la única señal de que los estadounidenses no compartían la urgencia de Machado por volver. El episodio que marcó los últimos meses de Machado fuera de Venezuela fue el que protagonizó tras el doble terremoto de junio, que dejó más de 6.500 muertos. Entonces intentó volver en dos ocasiones desde Centroamérica, y en ambas la maniobra fue frenada por altos funcionarios estadounidenses. Preguntado entonces por el episodio, Donald Trump lo negó: “No… no, para nada… ¿Cómo le voy a decir eso? Ella es increíble. Es una persona maravillosa”.

Washington, hasta entonces, alegaba preocupaciones por la seguridad de la política a su llegada al país. Luego, el propio secretario de Estado de Estados Unidos, Marco Rubio, dijo que podía volver cuando quisiera, “como cualquier ciudadana venezolana”. Mientras Delcy Rodríguez estaba en Nueva York en la Asamblea de las Naciones Unidas, la dirigente volvió a intentarlo sin éxito una quinta, sexta y séptima vez.

Fundadora de Vente Venezuela, Machado había salido del país a comienzos de diciembre de 2025, tras más de un año y medio en la clandestinidad, en un arriesgado periplo que la llevó disfrazada por las autovías del occidente venezolano y luego, en una embarcación precaria y con lesiones incluidas, en alta mar hacia Curazao, rumbo a Oslo, donde recibiría el Nobel de la Paz.

Inhabilitada para las presidenciales de 2024 —en las que el chavismo se proclamó vencedor pese a las actas que demostraban lo contrario— Machado se había convertido en el principal soporte de la candidatura de consenso de Edmundo González Urrutia, considerado el ganador real de aquellos comicios con el 70% de los votos.

World.title: El regreso de María Corina Machado busca acelerar la transición y retar al chavismo
World.content:
María Corina Machado ha regresado a Venezuela. Lo ha hecho por tierra, el último medio de transporte que le quedaba, después de haberlo intentado por aire y por mar al menos siete veces en los últimos 10 meses. Su mensaje de regreso lo ha publicado desde Barquisimeto, en el occidente del país, donde su primera aparición pública ha sido en el santuario de la Virgen de la Divina Pastora, uno de los puntos de peregrinación religiosa más importantes de Venezuela. “Estoy aquí. Con ustedes”, publicó crípticamente en su cuenta de X minutos después de que la información sobre su regreso empezase a circular. Sus primeras imágenes la muestran rodeada de gente.

Más información El regreso de María Corina Machado a Venezuela, en vivo

Su retorno es un desafío al chavismo en toda regla, aunque el oficialismo lleva semanas diciendo que el veto a su vuelta no ha salido de sus filas. Para los hermanos Jorge y Delcy Rodríguez y para Diosdado Cabello, la dirigente a la que sus seguidores ven como una mesías es, ante todo, un factor de desestabilización, y su llegada amenaza el equilibrio que han logrado mantener bajo el imperativo tutelaje de Washington.

En privado, el chavismo apuesta por el desgaste: sin capacidad para resolver los problemas cotidianos de los venezolanos, argumentan, la estrategia de movilización de la opositora acabará volviéndose en su contra. Es una apuesta incierta porque el efecto de su retorno en las calles es todavía bastante imprevisible, así como el papel que le reserva Estados Unidos. No está claro qué ha pactado Machado con Washington ni hasta dónde está dispuesta la Casa Blanca a respaldar a una figura que hasta hace poco parecía estorbar sus planes.

Todavía no se conocen los detalles de su regreso, una promesa que la líder opositora llevaba haciendo casi desde que salió clandestinamente del país el pasado mes de diciembre para recoger su Nobel de la Paz. Como suele ser habitual en su entorno, se mantiene el hermetismo, aunque fuentes de su partido Vente Venezuela, que han preferido mantener su nombre en la reserva, han asegurado que el retorno cuenta con la luz verde de los Estados Unidos, una aprobación “concedida de manera súbita”.

La agenda de trabajo de Machado “está en construcción”, pero se da por descontado que la opositora empezará su propia campaña de cara a unas futuras elecciones —sean municipales, legislativas o presidenciales— y llamará a un acuerdo nacional. “Lo primero que va a hacer es reunirse con la dirigencia del partido y el resto de los partidos de la oposición”. Su segundo paso será iniciar una gira nacional, según su entorno.

La dirigente regresa en plena negociación de un sector de la oposición con el chavismo y apenas días después de haber presionado, con movilizaciones en varias ciudades del país, para exigir una fecha electoral. En esas manifestaciones también se reclamó la lentitud de la mesa de diálogo impulsada por Washington y que lideran el presidente de la Asamblea Nacional y hermano de la presidenta, Jorge Rodríguez, y la opositora Dinorah Figuera.

El pasado jueves, durante la misma jornada de las manifestaciones, Delcy Rodríguez recibía a Figuera en lo que se consideró un espaldarazo del oficialismo —y también de Estados Unidos— a la hoja de ruta marcada para una transición democrática que incluye la reforma de la justicia y los organismos electorales antes de lanzarse a una convocatoria electoral. La presidenta interina aprovechó el encuentro para remarcar las corrientes opositoras y desconocer el liderazgo de Machado. “Todavía hay grupos muy, pero muy, pequeños, que se resisten y creen que pretendiendo incendiar el país y trancando calles es la vía para que Venezuela salga adelante. Yo reconozco a los venezolanos de bien que desde este diálogo impulsan cambios necesarios”, dijo.

Los planes de Machado se han ido reconfigurando desde que salió del país en diciembre pasado, luego de pasar más de un año en la clandestinidad. Después del 3 de enero, Machado pasó de negarse a negociar con el chavismo a ofrecerse a liderar las negociaciones con Delcy Rodríguez para conducir el país a una transición. Su figura, sin embargo, quedó relegada de todos los espacios de negociación creados por Estados Unidos, mientras la Administración de Trump iba estrechando su relación con el chavismo, que en su momento dejó claro que Machado tiene que rendir cuentas ante la justicia por, según le acusan, instigar la intervención militar extranjera.

Con información de Alonso Moleiro.

World.title: Trump, sobre el regreso de Maria Corina Machado a Venezuela: “Espero que esté a salvo, es una mujer muy agradable”
World.content:
El secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, aseguró hace un mes en la ONU que “el proceso de transición política ya está en marcha”

El presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, no tardó en reaccionar tras conocer la noticia del regreso de la líder opositora María Corina Machado a Venezuela tras un año de exilio. En sus primeras declaraciones desde la Casa Blanca aseguró: “Es una mujer muy agradable. Me entregó su Premio Nobel, así que ¿qué otra cosa puedo decir? Espero que esté a salvo", dijo el mandatario republicano antes de emprender viaje para participar en un mitin electoral en Michigan. “Nos está yendo realmente bien en Venezuela”, apostilló a preguntas de los periodistas. Unos minutos antes, cuando le preguntaron sobre el regreso de Machado, Trump reconoció desconocer su movimiento. “No sé nada sobre ello”, indicó, desvelando que no estaba informado sobre el último y exitoso intento de la líder opositora venezolana para regresar a su país.

El secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, que tampoco celebró el regreso de la líder opositora explícitamente, ha explicado que el regreso de Machado a Venezuela se debe al proceso de transición democrática que está tutelando Estados Unidos. “Las condiciones que permiten el regreso seguro de la señora Machado a Venezuela son el resultado directo de las conversaciones de reconciliación apoyadas por EE UU, que ya han logrado la liberación de cientos de presos políticos y el retorno del exilio de cientos de figuras de la oposición política”, ha escrito a través de una publicación en la red social X.

El equivalente estadounidense a ministro de Exteriores ha dejado clara su voluntad de mantener el proceso de transición para que puedan celebrarse elecciones sin que haya represalias por parte del Gobierno. “Estados Unidos espera que las libertades de todos los sectores de la política venezolana sigan siendo respetadas”.

Además, lanzó un mensaje al Ejecutivo venezolano para que participara en el cambio político. “Esperamos que todos los actores políticos apoyen estas conversaciones, que representan la mejor oportunidad que Venezuela ha tenido en treinta años de lograr pacíficamente no solo una elección libre y justa, sino una democracia duradera”. Delcy Rodríguez fue miembro del gabinete de Nicolás Maduro que mantuvo políticas represivas contra la oposición.

Trump no olvida la medalla del Nobel

Trump suele referirse en términos elogiosos hacia la líder opositora venezolana, aunque ha dejado clara su postura de apoyar al Gobierno de transición de Delcy Rodríguez, aupada al poder tras la detención de Nicolás Maduro en una operación militar relámpago a principios de este año. Desde entonces, Washington mantiene una cierta relación de tutela sobre Caracas.

El líder republicano siempre agradece que Machado le entregara la medalla que recibió tras ganar el Premio Nobel de la Paz hace exactamente un año. Esta semana, durante un acto electoral en Fort Myers (Florida), volvió a recordar: “Ella me dio su Premio Nobel, algo que no olvidaré, María”, dijo ante una audiencia repleta de cubanos y venezolanos exiliados.

El 10 de octubre del año pasado, María Corina Machado ganó el Premio Nobel de la Paz. El 10 de octubre del año pasado, María Corina Machado ganó el Premio Nobel de la Paz. En enero viajó a Washington para entregarle en la Casa Blanca la medalla del premio a Trump. El presidente estadounidense había hecho campaña para recibir el galardón, que ya obtuvo en su momento el expresidente Barack Obama. El actual ocupante del Despacho Oval argumentó que se merecía el premio porque aseguraba falsamente que había puesto fin a ocho guerras. Pero nunca obtuvo el reconocimiento por parte del Comité Noruego del Nobel.

Lo que sí logró fue la medalla acreditativa del premio. Machado se la regaló en el Despacho Oval y Trump no olvida aquel gesto. Suele decir que fue “un gran honor”. Y habla en términos elogiosos de la venezolana, pero mantiene a Delcy Rodríguez en el poder y echa balones fuera cuando le preguntan por la convocatoria de elecciones en el país caribeño.

De hecho, hace un mes aseguró que el país latinoamericano no está preparado aún para celebrar elecciones. “No creo que estén preparados todavía. Es [un gobierno venezolano] muy nuevo; los sacamos de una dictadura y nos llevamos muy bien con el gobierno. Delcy, como saben, está haciendo un trabajo muy, muy bueno. Es muy respetada y nosotros queremos eso [elecciones] y ellos también lo quieren. Delcy lo quiere, pero todavía no están preparados”, dijo.

Para lo que sí parecían estar preparados era para firmar un acuerdo con Estados Unidos para ceder parte de las reservas de petróleo, un total de 65.000 millones de barriles, para que la primera potencia mundial pueda engordar sus reservas estratégicas de crudo. Sea cual sea el cambio que se produzca en Venezuela, Washington querrá preservar el acuerdo y la relación privilegiada que mantiene sobre la industria petrolera de la isla caribeña.

A pesar de los elogios, la Administración Trump tampoco se mostró comprensiva con los intentos de la premio Nobel por regresar a Venezuela. Antes de su llegada tuvo varios intentos fallidos. Un portavoz del Departamento de Estado calificó esas intentonas como “contraproducentes” porque los esfuerzos debían dedicarse a los trabajos de rescate de los terrenos ocurridos en Venezuela a finales del pasado junio.

El secretario de Estado, Marco Rubio, se ha mostrado algo más conciliador. Hace un mes, durante la Asamblea General de la ONU, pronunció un discurso en el que afirmó que el futuro de Venezuela debe pasar por unas elecciones democráticas. “Debe haber un proceso de transición política, el cual ya está en marcha. Los dirigentes de la Asamblea Nacional de 2015 han estado dialogando regularmente con las autoridades interinas para sentar las bases y reconstruir las instituciones necesarias para celebrar elecciones libres y justas en Venezuela, lo cual es fundamental”, dijo desde Nueva York.

World.title: Primeras imágenes del regreso de María Corina Machado a Venezuela tras 10 meses fuera del país
World.content:
La dirigente opositora ha sido recibida en una iglesia de Barquisimeto, al noroeste, tras anunciarlo en redes sociales

La dirigente opositora y Premio Nobel de la Paz, María Corina Machado ha sido recibida por sus seguidores en una iglesia católica ubicada en el pueblo de Santa Rosa, Barquisimeto, al noroeste del país, tras poner fin a más de 10 meses fuera de Venezuela.

En las imágenes de su regreso, difundidas por su equipo de comunicación en redes sociales, se ve a la opositora saludando a los presentes en la misa después de anunciar en redes sociales que estaba de regreso.

La vuelta de la líder de la oposición antichavista se produce tras al menos siete intentos en los últimos tres meses.

World.title: More sleep on Sunday as clocks go back an hour
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Everyone is due an extra hour’s sleep on Sunday as the clocks will roll back an hour at 3am to 2am.

Daylight saving time in the Netherlands has been in place since 1977, following the oil crisis of the 70s, when saving energy on lighting became a priority.

The clocks go forward in spring, on the last Sunday of March, to give lighter evenings. Staying on summer time into the winter would mean very dark mornings, so in October the clocks return to standard time.

The EU has debated ending daylight saving time altogether and the European Parliament voted to stop it in 1996 but member states have not yet committed to it.

So tomorrow you can lie in a little longer.

The Dutch embassy in Cairo has closed to the public until further notice after nine days of protests outside the building, during which staff had to be evacuated, the embassy has announced on social media.

The demonstrators are demanding the release of Ahmed Nasser, deputy head of a pro-government Egyptian youth group, who was arrested in the Netherlands on October 10.

He was reportedly detained on suspicion of threatening Anas Habib, an Egyptian activist who lives in the Netherlands, and his pre-trial detention has been extended by 14 days, broadcaster NOS reported.

Habib drew international attention last summer when he filmed himself padlocking the gates of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague, in protest at the Egyptian government keeping the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed.

His action sparked similar protests at Egyptian embassies in more than 16 countries, after which supporters of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi began gathering outside embassies to “protect” them.

Days after Nasser’s arrest, Egyptian foreign minister Badr Abdelatty called his Dutch counterpart to demand his release and better protection for Egypt’s embassy in The Hague.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said on social media that the two had “discussed the need for progress on the security of our respective embassies and consular affairs.”

It is unclear exactly how Nasser is alleged to have threatened Habib.

World.title: Getting home safely: ADE festivals step up protection measures
World.content:
With the Amsterdam Dance Event (ADE), the world’s biggest electronic music event, underway, extra safety measures have been put in place by festival organisers and the city to make sure, Amsterdam says, that everyone feels “safe in the nightlife scene – free from any form of harassment, violence, discrimination, or (sexual) misconduct.”

To that end, there is a host of initiatives at various festival sites where techno lovers can recharge or get help getting home safely.

Bike buddies, hosts and Check-Ins

At the DGTL festival on NDSM island, cycling buddies will be on hand to help people get safely back and forth to the ferries. They will be working in pairs to ensure their own safety.

A Safe Check-In on NDSM wharf will be open all night for people who need physical help, feel unsafe at night or just need a breather. Phones can also be charged there.

At Awakenings in Halfweg, a Goodbye Host will be stationed at the exit, keeping a watchful eye on partygoers leaving solo. Hosts can help with route planning, and phones can also be charged here.

Both locations will also feature an Awareness Crew, trained teams identifiable by badges or vests that offer support to those feeling uncomfortable or unsafe.

Taking back the night

Some of the safety measures are not new. Last year, following the August murder of teenager Lisa while she cycled home alone and the resulting Take Back the Night campaign, the biking buddies programme was set up.

“We’ve been running social safety measures at our events since Covid, through our awareness teams and social safety hub, so this is something we’ve prioritized for a long time already,” Nikki Schuurs, who deals with Social Safety at DGTL, told Dutch News.

“Bike Buddies, however, was indeed introduced in response to the Take Back the Night campaign, following the murder of Lisa. Safety doesn’t stop at the dance floor.”

Visitors can find the Bike Buddy meeting point just outside the event. Group rides depart every 30 minutes between 21:00 and 07:00, on the hour and half-hour.

Safety concerns have again risen in the city following the violent death of 29-year-old Hajar, whose body was found in a suitcase in the Amstel River last week. She had last been seen cycling with a man near the RAI convention centre. He has since been arrested in connection with her death.

World.title: Inburgering with Dutch News: the great cycle path squeeze
World.content:
You can’t have failed to notice that Dutch cycle paths are no longer the preserve of old-fashioned cyclists. E-bikes, fatbikes, scooters, snorfietsen, speed pedelecs, disabled vehicles – a seemingly never-ending stream of other road users have moved in. But what exactly are the rules and regulations?

Lesson 64: what is allowed on the cycle path?

Fatbike

The fatbike, with its characteristic thick tyres and frequently thick riders, has become wildly popular. It’s not surprising because at the moment, riders do not need a helmet, driving licence, or third-party liability insurance. The fatbike is officially an e-bike, and therefore there is no age limit, but measures are afoot to make helmet-wearing compulsory for riders up to the age of 18.

Fatbikes are allowed to travel at up to 25 kph. However, many are doctored to go faster – as you will notice when you see them whizzing past cars that keep to the 30 kph limit, mandatory for cars in some Dutch cities.

Electric bike

The electric non-fat bike, so to speak, is literally overtaking the person-powered bike, and that is partly due to its popularity among older riders – who are also well represented in the annual traffic death toll. The same rules of the road as apply to fatbikes apply to ordinary e-bikes – none. You will, however, see more and more elderly riders with a helmet.

Electric cargo bike

The cargo bike, or moedermobiel, deserves a separate mention because of the riders’ mistaken opinion that everyone has to make way for this space-hogging vehicle because it carries cute little toddlers. A good place to spot cargo bikes is outside primary schools at 3pm, when they cause a veritable jam of their own.

Speed pedelec

Speed pedelecs are electric bikes as well, but unlike normal electric bikes, they can legally reach speeds of up to 45 kph. This makes them motorcycles in the eyes of the law, with the rules that then apply, such as mandatory helmet-wearing, a driving licence and insurance. Speed pedelecs can travel on cycle paths, but only at a maximum of 25 kph.

Snorfiets, or moped

No pedalling is needed for this motorised bike or moped, which has a maximum speed limit of 25 kph and is allowed on cycle paths. Although snorfietsen have the same speed limit as electric bikes, they are technically considered to be motorcycles, and riders need a helmet, a driving licence and insurance.

The introduction of helmets for all types of mopeds several years ago led to the downfall of the snorfiets – after all, if you need a helmet, why not drive a proper motorbike – or a fatbike?

Scootmobiel

The motorised wheelchair or scootmobiel is possibly the most dangerous vehicle on the cycle path. According to statistics agency CBS, the traffic death rate among mobility scooter riders is over six times that of motorbike riders and over 20 times that of cyclists.

Users don’t need to pass any tests or learn the rules of the road, and they can go pretty much wherever they like – shopping centre, pavement, cycle path, ordinary road – just not the motorway.

The Canta

The Canta looks like a brommobiel – a small electric vehicle with four wheels – but because it is considered a mobility aid for people with a disability, it is treated in the same way as a scootmobiel.

The Canta is not supposed to go faster than 30 kph on the cycle path and 45 kph on the road, but is allowed to mount the pavement and annoy pedestrians at 6 kph. It can also park anywhere and does not need a number plate.

The minimum age is 16, and you’ll need to take out insurance, but you don’t need a driving licence. The Canta became popular with youngsters who could not be bothered to cycle and has since spawned a surge in far hipper micro cars.

Micro cars

The Birò and its ilk are small, fashionable and, according to many, extremely annoying electric vehicles which are banned from cycle paths but whose drivers use them anyway – particularly as a sneaky escape when faced with a traffic jam.

Popular with estate agents and PR people, micro cars have a maximum speed of 45 kph. If you want one, you will need a brommobiel driving licence and must be 16 or over.

Electric scooter

The step, or scooter, used to be a children’s plaything, but since the invention of the electric version, they have been taking over cities throughout Europe. Steps which have been officially approved have been allowed on Dutch cycle paths since July 1 this year. In Dutch terminology they are known as “light electric vehicles”.

The step has a maximum speed of 25 kph, and riders have to be 16 or over. You will need third-party liability insurance, and the base must have a number plate which is clearly visible.

The e-step is predicted to rival the fatbike in popularity and ability to provoke cycle-path rage – as long as helmets are not compulsory.

World.title: Amsterdam exploring single-use packaging ban
World.content:
Amsterdam is considering banning single-use packaging, including coffee cups, fast-food containers and other single-use plastics that it says make up 30% of the city’s litter.

“Litter is a persistent problem; it is a symptom of a ‘throwaway society’ that pollutes our beautiful city and costs millions every year,” said Amsterdam executive Lian Heinhuis, who is responsible for waste and sanitation, in a statement.

“Yet the solution is within reach: putting an end to the throwaway culture.”

To that end, the city has commissioned a study into what it can legally do to tackle the problem. According to CircuLaw, which provides legal information on circular transitions, such a ban could be implemented, but only after less restrictive measures have proven not to work.

A ban also works best alongside other measures, such as a reliable supply of reusable packaging and a well-established return system.

The city says it will work with business owners and residents and also look at how other cities are managing the problem, including Copenhagen and Lisbon, the latter of which has already implemented a single-use packaging ban.

“Single-use packaging is a major problem,” the city said. “The plastics used in these items take hundreds of years to decompose – if they ever do at all. They pollute the soil and groundwater for a very long time, despite being used for an average of only about seven minutes.”

World.title: Student union furious as minister says interest cap unaffordable
World.content:
Despite a coalition promise to cap student loan interest rates at 2.5%, education minister Rianne Letschert has told parliament that the government can no longer afford to stick to its pledge.

The minister said that capping the interest rate at 2.5% is risky and expensive, and that the €40 million annual budget the coalition had set aside to cover the cap is only a quarter of what it would actually cost – €160 million – and could lead to other cuts in the education budget.

“I understand the concerns of current and former students regarding the rise in interest rates on student debt, driven by global instability and an increase in long-term interest rates,” Letschert said in a statement on Thursday.

“Unfortunately, I must conclude that it is not possible to implement a 2.5% interest rate cap with the €40 million per year that has been set aside. I find this very disappointing.”

Geopolitical costs

Since the coalition agreement was first presented at the end of January, the global landscape has significantly shifted due to geopolitical tensions and financial uncertainty. Long-term interest rates – to which student loan rates are linked – have risen from 2.7% to 3.3% and could climb higher.

“Recent shocks in the financial markets highlight just how unpredictable – and potentially financially risky – this interest rate policy is,” the ministry said.

But students aren’t buying it. “This effectively sends students out into the world burdened by an incredibly heavy backpack of debt,” LSVB, the national student union, told news service ANP. “The only certainty this cabinet offers students is the assurance that interest rates will rise even further in the coming years.”

Student union ISO added that once again, “students are the victims of empty promises.”

Letschert will discuss the issue with parliament later this month.

World.title: Cyber security centre warns PHP hacking situation could worsen
World.content:
The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is investigating the first signs of successful hacks on websites following the exposure of critical vulnerabilities on the web, and says the situation could “rapidly worsen”.

A spokesperson told the Volkskrant on Thursday that the signals came from the NCSC’s international network, and that there was no sign yet of abuse involving Dutch websites. The centre is still checking whether the reports are accurate.

Cybersecurity researchers, working with the help of AI, found that PHP, the programming language on which a majority of the web is built, had at least two serious vulnerabilities in its code.

Details of the weaknesses were leaked online on Monday, and the PHP developers announced they would issue an upgrade by Wednesday afternoon.

Hacking attempts began even before the leak, with Amazon reporting an attack attempt on October 17. US internet security firm Cloudflare said it saw hacking attempts run from thousands before the upgrade to millions afterwards.

Initially, the NCSC said that there were no signs of active hacks and the PHP developers said there were no indications of breaches.

Large amounts of government, healthcare and news sites were forced to go dark temporarily while awaiting the upgrade, including Dutch News.

The Netherlands was fast to act, closing a large amount of its sites and issuing warnings early on Wednesday, after which governments in Belgium, Germany, France and Finland did the same. The issue is now a global concern.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP said on Thursday it had not yet received any reports of data breaches linked to the vulnerabilities.

World.title: Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here) Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now. No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September. He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government. The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border. However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024 Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision. The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy. Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week. The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland. Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out. Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves. Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”. Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII. On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024 This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship. Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions. In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning. Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago. Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022 Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland. If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation. This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands. Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute. Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026 Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken. As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful. But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance. World.title: Leader of junior coalition partner quits Polish government
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. World.title: Protesters return to Poland’s streets demanding liberalisation of abortion law
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws. However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020. Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS — Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026 In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections. When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition. Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear. Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose. “It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.” In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”. Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw — Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026 The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023. Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition. World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.
